articles.title_orig: US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
articles.title_zh: US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
articles.content_orig:
US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
A US judge has temporarily blocked the deportation of a Venezuelan man who was shot by immigration agents in Texas, his lawyer says.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is being held in a detention centre with a bullet in his back, according to his lawyer. Judge Orlando Garcia, a Clinton appointee, scheduled a hearing for Garces Perez to appear in court in person next week.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement that an "illegal alien" had been the subject of a targeted vehicle stop but pushed back against suggestions he had been given inadequate medical care.
The incident comes months after a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man in Houston.
Garces Perez's immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, has filed a federal lawsuit for a temporary restraining order to prevent his removal from the country.
Since the judge ordered that her client appear in person on 30 September, he cannot be deported before then, she said.
"For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on social media.
"This is an important step, but our work is not over," she wrote. "Wilber still needs appropriate medical care, and we will continue fighting to protect his rights."
The gunshot fractured his clavicle and he is wearing a sling while having "significant swelling and pain," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
The cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced has not yet been determined, she said.
A spokesperson for US Attorney's Office in Texas declined to comment on the case.
The ICE agent who shot him - who joined the agency last year - was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, sources told the BBC’s US partner CBS News.
The Austin Police Department released footage from officers responding to the scene, but did not show what led to the incident.
On Tuesday, DHS pushed back against what it called "false narratives" surrounding what had happened, blaming sanctuary cities and media for "spreading lies" and discouraging people from resisting officers and evading arrest.
"Contrary to their claims, this person is an illegal alien who has no legal status to be here and has been given some of the best medical care he's ever received in his life," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a statement to the BBC.
DHS said the man, whom they did not name, was "the subject of a targeted vehicle stop" and that his work permit expired last year.
"No amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job by removing dangerous illegal aliens from our communities and making America safe again," Mullin said.
The Austin Police Department, which was not involved in the incident, released dashcam and body camera footage on Tuesday showing its officers at the scene.
It does not show the shooting, but several gunshots can be heard in one dashcam clip, while another shows officers approaching Garces Perez's car and detaining him. At one point, Garces Perez's t-shirt is cut to reveal what appears to be a single gunshot in his back.
Lincoln-Goldfinch previously told the BBC that after being unable to move his arm in the detention facility, Garces Perez was taken back to hospital on Monday evening. He was treated there and has since been returned to the detention facility.
He said he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during his transfer, despite his injury, she said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch added that detention personnel had revoked his communication privileges and moved him from an infirmary into an isolated room with a flat, non-adjustable bed.
In its statement on Tuesday, DHS said Garces Perez had received medical care "around the clock" and denied claims he received no pain medication and was forced to sleep on the floor.
"This alien was released from the hospital and arrived at the detention facility just a few hours later, where he slept on a bed," DHS said.
Texas lawmaker Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, on Tuesday demanded the Venezuelan national's release from detention.
Local and state officials have pushed for an independent investigation into the shooting, which occurred just before on Sunday afternoon.
Hours later, dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave the city.
DHS said on Tuesday that ICE "will not be slowing down nor leaving Austin".
The man's lawyer told US media he was making a DoorDash delivery when an unmarked black truck sideswiped his car.
He did not know the truck was an ICE vehicle and made a U-turn, she said. His car was hit again before agents got out and shot him, according to the attorney.

articles.title_orig: Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs
articles.title_zh: Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs
articles.content_orig:
No surprise here: “Patient Zero,” the song Taylor Swift announced Tuesday, is not an orphan or a one-off. The pop superstar followed news of the single a day later with her Wednesday morning reveal for a release that includes four new tracks and will also be out this Friday — “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore.”
A visit to pre-order pages shows that the new songs, besides the already announced “Patient Zero,” are “Cleveland!,” “Pink Clouding” and “Babylon,” listed as tracks 13-16 on the newly expanded version of her 2025 “Showgirl” album.
On social media, Swift wrote, “About a year ago, you guys did a truly unfathomable thing. Something that completely blew my mind… You gave ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ the biggest first week for an album in history. I took a trip to Sweden to celebrate with Max and Shellback, my two collaborators on this album. Really we just wanted to reflect and take in how grateful we were for the moment we were in, but there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: We wrote more songs. I hope you love them, because they were born out of pure gratitude for your exuberance for and celebration of the album we made. ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ including four new songs is out on Friday and available to pre-order and save now.”
Swifties had long assumed there would be no deluxe or bonus-filled edition of 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl” because, at the time, Swift had assured fans that she felt pleased with the exact 12-song configuration she was putting out and did want to augment it with anything she might have left on the cutting room floor. But, as fans now learn, that didn’t preclude coming up with additional material after the fact, which the singer is saying came out in a spontaneous explosion of post-release exhilaration with her two collaborators on that album.
Prior to “Showgirl,” she hadn’t worked with the dynamic duo of Max Martin and Shellback since 2018’s “Reputation,” but clearly the reunion took in a big way.
Eagle-eyed Swifties noted that Swift had quietly teased this project some time ago, by including the phrase “Patient for the encore” to the side of the frame in her music video for the “Showgirl” single “Opalite.”
Much more recently, she had given fans Easter eggs in puzzle form with a pre-taped sketch that aired as part of the Emmys telecast. There; Swift, in character as a “Law & Order: SVU” detective, said, “I think what we’re going to be looking for is hiding in plain sight.” She then stared into the camera and uttered several seeming nonsense phrases or words: “Saccharide. Aries. From the vineyard. North or south.” Fans eventually figured out that if you took the third letter from each of those utterances, they gave up the letters that form the word “encore.”
The announcement of the “Encore” edition also settles another point of trivia that had come up when Swift revealed the “Patient Zero” single was imminent on Tuesday. Many pointed out that Swift was not lately in the habit of releasing a stand-alone single ahead of an album actually coming out; the last time she had done so was with “Me!” being released months ahead of “Lover” in 2019. Now that everyone knows the “Encore” collection is coming out the same hour as the single, it’s clear she’s not breaking with that recent pattern after all.
The new release features cover photography by the team of fashion photographers Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott, continuing the imagery they created ffor the original “Showgirl” album.
No physical release has been announced for the expanded project, which hits DSPs as Thursday night turns into Friday morning. The streaming service Apple Music does show the track list as being broken down into Disc 1 (the original 12 tracks) and Disc 2 (the four newly released songs), but it’s unclear if that augurs for a two-disc vinyl or CD edition. Spotify has the 16 tracks listed in a single running order.
For now, the release of the four “Showgirl” addenda puts to bed previous widespread conjecture that Swift was certain to put out “Taylor Swift (Taylor’s Version)” this fall to celebrate the 20th anniversary of her debut album. But setting that aside for newly written songs is a tradeoff most fans will be happy with. So, “Our Song (Middle Aged Version)” can wait.

articles.title_orig: DOJ defends Trump White House media ban, citing national security and "professionalism and decorum"
articles.title_zh: DOJ defends Trump White House media ban, citing national security and "professionalism and decorum"
articles.content_orig:
DOJ defends Trump White House media ban, citing national security and "professionalism and decorum"
Washington — Justice Department lawyers on Tuesday defended President Trump's move to bar three news outlets from the White House over coverage of his administration, arguing that their reporting raises national security concerns and claiming their journalists failed to act with "professionalism and decorum."
In a filing with a federal district court in Washington, D.C., the Trump administration argued the president's ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico is legally sound. Reporters from those news organizations were stripped of their press credentials, also called "hard passes," denying them access to the White House grounds.
"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Justice Department lawyers wrote.
The Trump administration argued the president's ban complies with the First Amendment, because the government has at least two "compelling reasons" for denying the reporters' access: enforcing "minimum standards of professionalism" for the press and protecting classified information.
"The President believes basic journalistic standards require calling, asking for comment, and providing a reasonable opportunity for a response," they said. "At a bare minimum, it is a significant violation of decorum to publish classified and sensitive national security information."
The Justice Department also submitted to the court letters from the White House press office, dated Tuesday, to each of the three outlets notifying them that the president decided to revoke their journalists' hard passes.
The letters claim that the news outlets have "exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."
The White House gave CNN, MS NOW and Politico a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to respond to its claims.
The letters appear designed to address the news outlets' claims that the ban deprived them of due process, since their reporters didn't receive advance notice that they would be denied access to the White House and an opportunity to be heard before revoking their credentials.
"The President provided no notice that he would immediately deny news organizations whose reporting he dislikes access to the White House grounds," lawyers for the organizations said in a filing. "His standard for denying access is arbitrary and vague — indeed, it can hardly be called a standard at all."
The Justice Department's response comes ahead of a hearing, set for Wednesday afternoon, during which a judge will consider whether to order the White House to restore the media organizations' credentials and access. CBS News and dozens of other news organizations have signed onto an amicus brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
The three news organizations sued Mr. Trump and top administration officials on Monday, calling his ban a "direct assault on the First Amendment" and a "blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles." The lawsuit names Mr. Trump and three of his top aides: Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff; Steven Cheung, White House communications director; and Sean Curran, the head of Secret Service.
The news outlets asked U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed to the federal bench by Mr. Trump during his first term, to rule quickly to once again allow them access to the White House.
The organizations argued in their court filings that the ban violates their due process rights because Mr. Trump "provided no notice" to the companies before banning them, and no opportunity for CNN, MS NOW, or Politico to oppose the ban before it was announced and reporters for the news outlets had their press credentials confiscated.
The ban, the organizations say, also violates the First Amendment because it "brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint," and "to coerce more favorable coverage of the administration from CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from reporting that the President might view as unfavorable."
Kelly oversaw a lawsuit brought by former CNN reporter Jim Acosta during the first Trump administration after the White House moved to revoke his press credential. The judge sided with Acosta after CNN sued and ordered his press pass to be restored, finding Acosta's due process rights under the Fifth Amendment had been violated. The White House complied with the order, and CNN dropped the lawsuit shortly afterward.
Mr. Trump has also barred The Associated Press from attending certain White House events after the news outlet refused to conform to Mr. Trump's proclamation that changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America."
The wire service sued on First Amendment grounds. While a federal judge in D.C. initially ruled that the White House must restore the news outlet's access, an appeals court later allowed the ban to take effect. The litigation in that case is ongoing.
The ruling from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit hinged on the fact that the AP was blocked from certain restricted spaces like the Oval Office and Air Force One that only a small subset of the White House press corps can access — a narrower policy than the outright ban imposed on CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
In a 2-1 decision, the two judges in the majority, Neomi Rao and Gregory Katsas, said the White House can't ban journalists from spaces that are "generally open to the press," like the briefing room, based on their viewpoint. Mr. Trump appointed both Rao and Katsas to the D.C. Circuit in his first term.
Since Mr. Trump returned to the White House for his second term, his press office assumed control of the press pool, a rotating group of journalists who cover the president every day and disseminate information and footage to thousands of other news outlets.
The president's ban has already disrupted that information flow: CNN is a member of the television pool system, which includes CBS News, ABC News, NBC News and Fox News, and was scheduled to travel with Mr. Trump to New York on Monday for the United Nations General Assembly.
But the network, which was set to provide coverage in the TV pool slot, was kicked off the trip because of the president's ban. As a result, the four other networks in the rotation decided to suspend the television pool altogether in solidarity with their CNN colleagues.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s approval plunges into the 20s, and Republicans give up
articles.title_zh: Trump’s approval plunges into the 20s, and Republicans give up
articles.content_orig:
With President Donald Trump at record unpopularity, Republicans are facing an even bleaker midterm political landscape than they did eight years ago, a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS finds.
Nationally, voters say they prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans by an eight-point margin – slightly more modest than their 12-point advantage in CNN’s September polling ahead of the 2018 midterms in Trump’s first presidency.
But Trump is even more unpopular than he was in 2018, and the economic backdrop has worsened considerably. In his first term, Trump saw net-positive ratings on the economy, which Americans largely saw as thriving. Now, just 27% of Americans approve of Trump on the economy, down 22 points from 2018. And 28% call economic conditions good – a drop of 41 points.
The issue has risen in prominence: Two-thirds of registered voters call the economy “extremely important” to their vote, higher than in the autumn before either of the past two midterms. And, in a shift from recent trends, Americans say they agree more with Democrats than Republicans when it comes to the issue.
That leaves a midterm electorate in which the president’s supporters are largely tepid, while his opponents are furious. In a midterm high for an incumbent president dating back to the George W. Bush era, 44% of registered voters say they view their congressional vote as a message of opposition to Trump. Just 19%, by contrast, say their vote will be a message of support for the president.
At the same time, the public remains split on what a Democratic congressional victory might mean for the cost of living in the US, or their own financial situation.
Support for Trump continues to erode
Overall, just one-third of Americans now approve of Trump’s job performance, the continuation of a steady decline throughout his second term. That’s on par with the 34% he saw in July, but marks a numeric low in either term of his presidency.
Only 13% now say they strongly approve of his performance, another career low. Just 24% say he has the right priorities, and a scant 20% approve of his handling of inflation.
Two-thirds of Americans say Trump has worsened economic conditions in the country, and majorities say that the war in Iran, as well as new tariffs, have had a negative effect on their own finances. By contrast, few say they’re seeing benefits from Trump policies like changes to the tax law, or the establishment of Trump Accounts for children born during his second term. Most Americans also call increased gas prices a financial hardship for their household – and though only about one-quarter call that hardship severe, the public remains dubious that Trump has any plan to address the issue.
A 57% majority of Americans say they feel uncertain about their own finances, with nearly half expressing stress about their financial future – a sentiment that’s particularly acute among younger adults. Just 31% of Americans say they feel hope and 23% that they feel security, down 8 and 7 points respectively from spring. More than one-third aren’t confident about maintaining their current standard of living, worse than the numbers at the tail end of the Great Recession.
While Republicans haven’t deserted Trump, relatively few remain enthusiastic about the current state of his presidency. Only 35% say they strongly approve of him, down from 66% in September 2018. In the latest poll, 50% of Republicans disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation, 59% say the Iran war has hurt their finances, and nearly half say he’s worsened or had no effect on economic conditions.
Democrats are fired up for the midterm, but the public’s expectations for a Democratic Congress aren’t high
Overall, voters say, 49% to 41%, that they’d support a Democratic candidate over a Republican candidate in their congressional district. Democratic and Democratic-leaning registered voters are 16 points likelier than GOP-aligned voters to say they’re extremely motivated to vote this year.
Among the full public, anger at Trump and deep dissatisfaction with the status quo are paired with real skepticism about the prospects of a Democratic-controlled Congress.
Both congressional Democrats and congressional Republicans are deeply – and about equally – unpopular, with about one-quarter of Americans approving.
And while Americans say by a 10-point margin that a Democratic-controlled Congress would have a positive effect on health care policy, they’re closely split on whether a change in power would be more positive or negative when it comes to the cost of living in the US, their own finances, corruption, or foreign policy.
But the Democrats are nevertheless seen as the lesser of two evils on a crucial issue: They lead the GOP by 7 points as the party Americans say is closest to their own views on the economy. Over the past four years, this is both by far the best number for Democrats and the worst for Republicans on the topic.
A 68% majority of voters call the economy “extremely important” to their vote, topping a list of more than 10 issues. That’s far higher than the 59% in fall 2022 or 44% in fall 2018 who called the issue extremely important.
The poll finds that elections themselves, election integrity and voting rights are also at the forefront of many partisans’ minds as Trump continues his efforts to reshape or cast doubt on parts of the voting system, with 61% calling the issue extremely important. Majorities also say that inflation and health care are extremely important, while other hot-button issues – including data centers and AI, abortion, and policies around gender identity and trans people – don’t register as deeply.
Voters’ decisions, though, aren’t always down to which issues they find most important – more than half of voters say that other factors will be more important in their vote for Congress this year. And in this year where discontent with Washington is at the forefront of many voters’ minds, about a third say their votes will be primarily driven by which party will control the House of Representatives, including almost 4 in 10 of the most motivated voters.
CNN’s Jennifer Agiesta, Edward Wu and Isabelle LaBianco contributed to this report.
The CNN poll was conducted by SSRS online and by telephone September 16-17 among a random national sample of 1,206 adults, including 867 registered voters. Results for the full sample have a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points; it is 4.1 points among registered voters.

articles.title_orig: Spotify is giving you the keys to its recommendation algorithm with US launch of 'Taste Profile'
articles.title_zh: Spotify is giving you the keys to its recommendation algorithm with US launch of 'Taste Profile'
articles.content_orig:
Spotify is giving listeners a new tool to shape the recommendations it delivers to their app’s Home feed.
The music streaming giant on Wednesday began rolling out a feature called “Taste Profile” to its Premium subscribers in the U.S. that allows users to see, for the first time, how Spotify understands their taste across music and other audio. Users can request changes using natural language commands to fine-tune their recommendations, or make broader changes.
Powered by Spotify’s AI, Taste Profile was unveiled in March at the SXSW conference in Austin by Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström. However, the feature was initially available in beta only to listeners based in New Zealand.
Now, the feature is arriving in Spotify’s largest market in terms of traffic and revenue, where it will be put to a larger test among listeners aged 18 and up.
In some ways, Taste Profile essentially gives you the keys to Spotify’s algorithm. It is how the streaming platform chooses what music and podcasts to suggest, including in its flagship Discover Weekly playlist, its Made for You recommendations, and the highly anticipated annual review known as Spotify Wrapped.
Though Spotify’s algorithmic understanding of a listener’s habits is largely credited as the secret to its success, those recommendations don’t always reflect users’ evolving tastes. The platform often ends up recommending too-similar music when a user would rather branch out.
Now, by editing their Taste Profile directly, Spotify users can request more variety or ask for more or less of a certain genre, artist, or overall vibe.
The feature could be used to remove recommendations based on music that users may regularly stream, but not necessarily care to see more of — for instance, sleep sounds played at night, or whatever music a teenager plays while in the car on their parent’s account.
Until now, Spotify has offered some options to remove music from your Taste Profile, but they only let you exclude certain tracks or playlists. More recently, the company added a much-requested toggle switch that would prevent kids’ music from impacting their parents’ recommendations.
To access Taste Profiles on the mobile app, first tap on your profile pic, then scroll down and select Taste Profile. From here, you’ll be able to explore how Spotify currently understands your taste across music, podcasts, and audiobooks. Under “Tell us more,” you’ll then enter what you’d like to adjust and send the message.
After a few hours, your app’s Home Page will reflect a different set of suggestions.
Spotify says the feature can be used when you want to explore a new genre or era, but aren’t sure where to start, or if you want to adjust the vibe of the music — like if you want more energizing tracks. You can also tell Spotify what sort of podcasts and audiobooks you want to better shape those recommendations.
The feature is still in beta. The company didn’t offer a timeline as to when it would reach a wider audience.

articles.title_orig: First Thing: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes
articles.title_zh: First Thing: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes
articles.content_orig:
Good morning. Donald Trump has used the platform of the UN general assembly in New York to threaten to “annihilate the Islamic republic” of Iran, “and do it quickly”. He called on countries to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices.
Despite his bombastic rhetoric, Trump also said Iranian officials held three hours of talks with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the meeting. Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June. A senior Iranian official also indicated that Iran was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week.
What else did Trump say at the UN? The president doubled down on his defence of AI development, saying warnings about runaway agents were a “hoax”; announced the US would build new military bases in Greenland; attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation”; and prompted the Cuba’s delegation to stage a walkout when he described the country as a “failed state”.
Did he continue his attacks on US media networks? Trump scolded a CNN anchor for covering him at the UN, saying “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Last week, the president announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House.
Follow UN proceedings live today here.
Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch
A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas.
John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”.
Where else is the president seeing dissent from Republicans? Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump.
Mississippi grand jury decides not to charge anyone in death of Nolan Wells
A grand jury made a unanimous decision to not bring criminal charges against anyone in the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teenager who died after a boat outing with friends on 4 July.
Wells’s case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the 18-year-old’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who did not return from the trip that day.
Hayden Panettiere’s cause of death confirmed as fentanyl overdose
Hayden Panettiere died from a fentanyl overdose, according to the Greenville county coroner’s office. Medical examiners said there were “no signs of trauma” and “the manner of death has been ruled accident”. Panettiere was in her South Carolina apartment with her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother Zach when she died on August 16.
Panettiere, known for her roles in television series including Heroes and Nashville, began acting at just 11 months old. After her death, her father released a statement, saying: “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”
Ella Langley’s hit song Choosin’ Texas has set a new record, spending 23 weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, unseating Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas Is You, which topped the charts for 22 weeks.
An US F-16 fighter jet in western Germany crashed on Tuesday, the US military said, adding that one pilot had ejected safely.
DoorDash said it would pay $131.5m to settle a New York City government investigation that found the food delivery company underpaid or waited too long to pay workers.
‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular has been charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts. The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, has been scheduled for a 14 October arraignment.
Qantas says travellers will be able to fly between Sydney and New York in just 18 hours from mid-2028 when the airline launches its second ultra long-haul route.
Stat of the day: Trump made more than 1,000 stock trades in July worth up to $270m
The president made more than 440 purchases and 700 sales despite voter anger over elected officials trading stocks.
Well Actually: Get tested and talk to your partner – how to have safer sex after age 50
We are long past the era when sex was for young married couples trying for children and nobody else. Amanda Zuckerman Klarsfeld has compiled this thoughtful selection of advice for older lovers.
Don’t miss this: Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised
The UK capital’s iconic red buses have a problem: they are getting slower. And it isn’t just an issue in London, but a growing worldwide problem for transit networks, with worrying implications for the poorest in society. Our visuals team have put together this rich explainer to explore why.
… or this: Will anyone topple soccer boss Infantino?
Since Fifa abandoned its controversial World Cup sell-off plan last month, causing deep divisions among the global administrators of soccer, the governing body’s president, Gianni Infantino, has continued to lobby for re-election. Matt Hughes analyses how he is trying to cling on after the debacle.
Climate check: Huge El Niño projected to cause 450,000 deaths in next six months
More than 450,000 people are projected to die from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño in the next six months, according to estimates by climate scientists. The toll is on top of the early deaths resulting from temperatures already driven up by the climate crisis. It will strike across the globe, including the US. Many further deaths are expected from the droughts, wildfires and flooding that El Niños bring.
Last Thing: My perilous, painful, perfect month of pilates
My colleague Sammy Gecsoyler has taken up pilates, and has written this very funny account of his month’s journey to better fitness and health.

articles.title_orig: Lost in translation: Israel, Huckabee blast Macron over Hamas comments as France clarifies wording
articles.title_zh: Lost in translation: Israel, Huckabee blast Macron over Hamas comments as France clarifies wording
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump offered a roaring counterbalance to a spate of world leaders bashing Israel or appearing to equivocate between the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attacks and Jerusalem’s response — as one world leader was assailed for his comments on Hamas.
Gaza dominated the opening day of the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday, despite a ceasefire, as world leaders accused Israel of continuing to displace Palestinians and undermine prospects for peace.
French President Emmanuel Macron accused Israel of violating Palestinian rights in the West Bank, questioning the justification for its actions and making a remark that was translated as "Hamas was never active in the West Bank."
MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT
Israeli U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon challenged his claim about Hamas’ presence in the West Bank. "French President Emmanuel Macron claimed from the UN podium that Hamas has ‘never been active’ in Judea and Samaria. Just two days ago, a French citizen was murdered there," Danon wrote on X. "Mr. President, Emmanuel Macron, do your homework before lecturing Israel. Check the facts."
Asked by Fox News Digital to clarify Macron’s remarks, a French Foreign Ministry spokesperson said: "The president meant to say that Hamas does not govern the West Bank. His remarks should therefore not be misinterpreted."
In response to the comments, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee reposted Israel's Minister of Diaspora and Combating Antisemitism. Huckabee stated, "Hard to imagine a more out of touch with reality speech than Macron at UN. @AmichaiChikli corrects the record. Hamas is an evil scourge, and they have killed innocent American citizens.
Chickli's post noted in part that, "Since 1990, Hamas has carried out more than 80 lethal terrorist attacks originating in or directed from Judea and Samaria, murdering more than 350 Israeli civilians." Judea and Samaria is another term used for the West Bank.
Macron also accused Israel of violating Palestinian rights in the West Bank and undermining the sovereignty of neighboring Lebanon, where he said villages in the south were being "razed." Macron questioned the credibility of the international community’s recognition of Palestinian statehood if it failed to act on the situation in Gaza. "Some claim that peace has been achieved," he said, calling the situation "shameful."
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, in his final address to the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) as secretary-general, opened fire on Israel’s response in Gaza, describing it as "a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as Secretary-General."
"Amid the turmoil engulfing the region, we must not lose sight of the devastating situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory," he said, as the world approaches three years since the Hamas terror attacks that sparked the Israeli military response he spent much of his speech criticizing.
At the same time, Guterres lamented the ongoing conflict in Sudan, saying the war-torn East African nation is a place the "world looks away" from wrongly.
Yet his decision to single out Gaza as "the worst" devastation he had witnessed during his tenure raised questions about the international community's uneven attention to two of the world's deadliest conflicts. Approximately 72,000 Palestinians have been reported killed in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run Health Ministry, compared with an estimated 150,000 people killed in Sudan's civil war. Many of those killed in Gaza include terrorists.
King Abdullah II of Jordan, a regional U.S. ally whose country signed a peace agreement with Israel in 1994, doubled down on the anti-Israel tenor, accusing Jerusalem of "war crimes."
"In my region, from Lebanon to Yemen, to Sudan, protracted conflict is deepening humanitarian suffering," Abdullah said. "And if anyone had any doubt that a crisis in our part of the world stays there, just look at the energy and grocery bills of ordinary families, from Mumbai to Madrid to Minnesota."
WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR?
Abdullah said Jordanian field hospitals had been targeted during the first 300 days of the "so-called ceasefire" and lamented the deaths of Palestinian children.
He also praised Trump for "pushing hard for peace" while pivoting to fault Israel for "moving the goalposts" and allegedly destroying civilian infrastructure in Gaza.
"The question is, is this the behavior of a democratic state governed by law? What is unfolding across the West Bank is not a series of isolated acts. It is elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land," Abdullah said.
"And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime."
Abdullah also accused Israel of harboring territorial ambitions in Syria, calling on the international community to act.
Just before Abdullah, President Donald Trump offered a scathing counterweight to the invective directed at the Netanyahu administration and Israel’s response to Palestinian terrorism.
BRITAIN’S DRAMATIC CRACKDOWN ON ISRAELI SETTLEMENTS SPARKS FIERCE RESPONSE AS US BLOWBACK LOOMS
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon" was a mantra repeated by Trump from the dais, as he noted that the Khamenei regime had also celebrated Oct. 7 as a "service to humanity" while murdering thousands of Iranian citizens in recent months, according to the president.
"Just imagine such a vile regime, wherever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront, the reality that far too many preferred to ignore," he said, taking occasional swipes at nations — and previous U.S. leaders — who refused to help neutralize the Iranian threat.
"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" he asked. "But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election," he added, suggesting Iran is waiting to see whether Republicans retain control of Congress while noting that he himself is not on the ballot.
Meanwhile, criticism of Israel continued from the dais throughout the day.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said that former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and former Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat were "statesmen" who sought solutions with courage and clarity.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"They were defeated by hatred," Lula da Silva claimed, according to the U.N.’s transcript of his remarks.
"Generations of Palestinians will carry the pain and trauma left by the genocide of women and children perpetrated by Netanyahu[‘s] government in Gaza," he said.
Danon told Fox News Digital that, "Unfortunately, it’s not new, but the U.N. is obsessed with Israel."
"Instead of focusing and dealing with the real issues, they all gather and gang against Israel," he said. "[It is] the weakness of the secretary general. That is why we are grateful for President Trump, who came to the U.N., delivered a very powerful speech with moral clarity, but we are used to it… Unfortunately, instead of taking practical actions to improve the world, it's much easier to blame Israel about everything," he said.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, called Gaza "the world's biggest graveyard for children" and compared the situation there to Holocaust-era concentration camps, continuing his history of comparing Israel to Nazi Germany.
Danon said it is legitimate to criticize Israel and that its leaders welcome debate — but that the U.N. instead delved into "pure hate [and] incitement," singling out Erdoğan, who is supposed to be a Western ally.
"[He] comes here every year, compares the Israelis to the Nazis. That's shameful. That's shameful. And he shows that he's an antisemite. He doesn't really care about the Palestinians. He just wants to sow chaos and instigate against the Jewish people."

articles.title_orig: Meta's Muse reignites AI disruption fears. Traders are targeting this brokerage stock as next casualty
articles.title_zh: Meta's Muse reignites AI disruption fears. Traders are targeting this brokerage stock as next casualty
articles.content_orig:
Meta's latest consumer AI product is sending such big shockwaves through the market that it's even inflaming a long-time rivalry in the brokerage business between 55-year old investing giant Charles Schwab, and Robinhood, an icon of the post-Covid trading boom among young investors.
Shares of Schwab fell 6% Tuesday, touching the lowest since early July and the stock is now down more than 8% since Meta announced Muse. Meanwhile, Robinhood's stock was higher, notching anotheryear-to-date high. In May, the company launched AI agents that can now trade and manage portfolios on behalf of users.
Shares of sprawling wealth management business LPL Financial Holdings dropped 7% Tuesday, financial services firm Raymond James Financial shed 3.5 percent, and Interactive Brokers slipped 1% as the State Street Financial Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLF) lost 2% and is now down 6 percent from highs made earlier this month. Higher interest rates may not be helping.
It's not the first time an AI product has jostled the group – in February, the same group of stocks dropped when tech platform Altruist said its platform `Hazel' can create tax-planning strategies for individuals and advisors. Schwab stock recovered some in the months after – LPL has not.
"Schwab's an interesting animal," said Jimmy Lee, founder and CEO of The Wealth Consulting Group, a Las Vegas-based advisor that oversees $8 billion in assets. "To us in the advisor space they're kind of neutral and figuring out how best to protect their market share. I don't think Meta brings a lot of competition from the custodian perspective because it's not like Altruist's platform, but there is a lot of disruption that's going to happen among financial middle-men that charge fees for billing, reporting, trading, etc."
Meta's AI assistant says it won't trade for users or give financial advice, but when queried with how it might mimic the work of a financial advisor or broker, lists abilities including tracking investments and progress towards goals, as well as analyzing how portfolio holdings fit together.
Last week, Schwab Advisor Services, the company's platform for registered investment advisors, announced it is working with Anthropic to create Claude for Financial Advisors. In May, the company launched an AI tool that includes tailored analysis from the company's research arm. Representatives from Schwab did not respond to a request for comment. Robinhood reps declined to add to this story.
Robinhood's bounce on Tuesday brings its stock to a 10% rally on the year after dropping more than 40% in the first three months. The retail-focused brokerage, which also offers digital banking and advisory services, is up 1200 percent the past three years. Schwab stock is up 83 percent and the XLF is up 65 percent.
"AI and tokenization threaten to dismantle the frictions that legacy financial intermediaries have historically monetized," Piper Sandler analyst Patrick Moley wrote in a note in April. "Schwab's reliance on low-yielding sweep cash puts it squarely in the crosshairs."
Bets increase against Schwab
Judging by options-market flows around the stocks on Tuesday, the threat to Schwab may be a lasting one.
Options volume in Schwab was more than five times the average, with nearly twice as many puts bought vs. calls, Cboe LiveVol data show. The most popular contract to buy was the 90-strike put expiring mid-January, a bet the stock drops another 13% the next three months. To be sure, there was one big counter-trade sale of the Oct. 16 95-strike puts.
What's arguably most notable is in Robinhood options, sentiment was the opposite – traders bought twice as many calls as puts with more than 80 percent of the $95 million in premium traded tied to calls. The most heavily traded contract was the 125-strike call expiring on Friday.
"Gen Z and millennials gravitate towards platforms like Robinhood and Public which is why those platforms ship products so quickly," Gav Blaxberg, founder of Wolf Financial, a popular online trader enclave, said in a call. "Robinhood has built enough trust rebuilding its brand since GameStop and they're allowing agents to trade literally everything."
Correction: The founder of Wolf Financial is Gav Blaxberg. An earlier version of this story misspelled his name.

articles.title_orig: As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
articles.title_zh: As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
articles.content_orig:
As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to agree to only limited cooperation on AI safety at summit.
As industry leaders urge a global slowdown in artificial intelligence development for the sake of humanity, the two superpowers driving the technology’s rapid advancement have given no indication they intend to hit the brakes.
The United States and China, which are locked in a fierce strategic rivalry, have each rebutted calls to slow the pace of AI development, even as industry executives and researchers stress the need for international cooperation to avoid exposing humans to catastrophic – or even existential – risks.
- list 1 of 4Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrives in New York for UNGA
- list 2 of 4Zelenskyy says Ukraine ready for energy truce with Russia after Trump talks
- list 3 of 4In Senegal, a mother’s ordeal exposes a health system under strain
- list 4 of 4South Sudan’s Kiir dissolves government ahead of first national elections
As US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare to meet on Wednesday in Washington, DC, for the third time this year, expectations for cooperation on AI safety are modest. Observers anticipated measures that, at best, would fall far short of the coordinated slowdown that many experts said is needed.
“The two countries host nearly all frontier labs and most of the models people download,” said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, describing agreed guardrails between the US and China as “close to a precondition” for safe AI.
“A safety regime covering one side’s models covers half the problem,” Wang Graylin said.
Hampering the prospects for US-China cooperation, analysts said, are mutual mistrust and divergent perceptions of the primary risks involved.
Trump has dismissed fears about AI as a “conspiracy” and suggested guardrails are not needed under his leadership, stressing the need for the US to stay ahead of China in the frontier technology.
Trump, who has cast AI dominance as crucial to the US maintaining its position as the top global power, on Tuesday again poured cold water on hopes for international cooperation, telling the United Nations General Assembly that Washington would oppose any “globalist scheme” to control AI.
China has taken a more hands-on approach to AI regulation – releasing the third iteration of its security framework this month – but has similarly rebuffed calls for a slowdown, dismissing fears of existential risks aired in Silicon Valley as “fearmongering”.
While Chinese officials have raised concerns about the dangers of AI, they have related it to more prosaic concerns, including cybersecurity and the authority of the ruling Communist Party.
In a rare essay this month, Chinese Minister of State Security Chen Yixin warned of “hostile forces” using AI to “fabricate political rumours” and “incite antagonistic sentiments”, threatening “political security, institutional security and ideological security”.
“China also increasingly recognises loss of control, misuse and cyber-risks but is much more sensitive to the possibility that ‘AI safety’ could become a justification for restricting Chinese access to chips, computers or markets,” said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
“So the deepest obstacle is whether both sides can separate genuine safety cooperation from the wider technology competition,” Sun said.
“If every safety discussion is linked to export controls or slowing China’s development, Beijing will naturally question the purpose of cooperation,” Sun added.
So far, the only proposals publicly floated by either side have been a US-China dialogue and a notification mechanism for reporting national security threats.
While those measures would be positive first steps, the US and China would still need to reach an agreement on the AI capabilities or uses that should be off-limits to avert the greatest threats, experts said.
There is no consensus within the AI sector about how the technology should be regulated – or even whether government-led supervision is needed at all.
While AI leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have called for a slowdown and greater regulation, some experts argued that such calls do not go far enough and development should be paused outright.
“International coordination is absolutely critical. We need more than safeguards,” said David Krueger, an assistant professor at the University of Montreal who specialises in AI safety.
“We need an immediate, indefinite international moratorium on frontier AI development.”
Other key figures, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, have played down the need for external oversight and emphasised AI’s potential to deliver transformative benefits for society.
Among those most alarmed at the rapid pace of AI development, recursive self-improvement, which describes when AI models learn to improve themselves, is often identified as a critical tipping point.
In an essay this month urging the AI sector to “pace the frontier”, Amodei said the US and China should discuss an agreement to “substantially limit” the rate of AI development while acknowledging that any deal is unlikely given the potential for a rule-breaking party to shift the global balance of power.
“The US and China must agree on AI capabilities red lines that will not be crossed. Most crucially, AI must never get powerful enough for recursive self-improvement,” said Otto Barten, director of the Netherlands-based Existential Risk Observatory.
“We do not know where the positive feedback loop of ever-smarter AIs creating ever-smarter AIs without human supervision will end and what these agents will finally be able to do,” Barten added.
Wang Graylin said Washington and Beijing should come to an agreement on what constitutes an “unacceptable capability” and a common standard to test frontier models, ideally by an independent international body that is funded by multiple countries.
But Wang Graylin acknowledged that distrust is clouding the prospects for an agreement and US officials are likely to see any deal as impossible to verify.
“Verification is hard for software you cannot see,” he said.
Sun said the US could ease the path to cooperation by “drawing a clearer line” between policies aimed at AI safety and those intended to maintain Washington’s technological advantage.
China could also contribute to greater trust by providing “greater transparency about its safety practices, model-evaluation methods and incident-reporting mechanisms,” Sun said.
Henry Gao, an expert on China and trade law at Singapore Management University, said a deeper issue is a fundamental mismatch in how Washington and Beijing view AI risks.
“Many in the US AI-safety debate focus on the possibility of highly capable AI escaping human control and posing catastrophic risks to humanity,” Gao said.
“In China, national security concerns appear more geopolitical: A major perceived danger is that the US could gain a decisive AI advantage and use it against China,” Gao said.
“That creates pressure to accelerate rather than slow development.”
Some AI experts argued that the focus of a US-China dialogue should be on mitigating existing risks rather than slowing development outright.
“AI is already extremely useful and has the potential to improve lives around the world,” said Rui Ma, a tech industry consultant and the founder of the Tech Buzz China news site, adding that pausing development would also impact the technology’s positive applications.
“I think thoughtful rules of engagement, constant monitoring, open channels of communication and the ability to adjust our approach as AI acquires different capabilities are much more important,” Ma said.
“The safeguards need to evolve alongside the technology.”

articles.title_orig: Vogue World Milan 2026 red carpet
articles.title_zh: Vogue World Milan 2026 red carpet
articles.content_orig:
Jennifer Lopez has officially arrived in Milan, and she is wasting no time delivering major fashion moments.
The 56-year-old star stepped out in the Italian fashion capital on September 22 during Milan Fashion Week, trading the menswear-inspired separates she wore upon her arrival for something considerably more dramatic. A voluminous black ball gown worthy of a modern-day princess.
Lopez was photographed making her way through Milan in the striking all-black creation, which featured a fitted, lingerie-inspired bodice with delicate lace and a romantic scalloped neckline.
From the waist, the silhouette dramatically expanded into a full tea-length skirt covered in dimensional black floral appliqués and shimmering embellishments.
The exaggerated volume gave the look the grandeur of a traditional ball gown, while its shorter hemline allowed Lopez's pointed black pumps to peek out underneath.
She pushed the regal aesthetic even further with sheer black opera gloves, transforming the monochromatic dress into a full Old Hollywood-meets-modern-royalty moment.
The jewels stole the show:
As dramatic as the gown was, Lopez's jewelry provided an unexpected burst of color.
The singer and actress wore an elaborate statement necklace featuring sparkling stones and a large turquoise-colored pendant that rested at the center of her décolletage. Coordinating earrings added even more sparkle, creating a vivid contrast against the otherwise entirely black ensemble.
The combination of the enormous skirt, opera gloves and colorful jewels made the outing feel worlds away from the relaxed tailoring Lopez wore when she first touched down in Milan.
For that earlier appearance, she paired an oversized white button-down shirt with a black bra, high-waisted wide-leg trousers, platform heels and a structured Dolce & Gabbana handbag. The look offered a daring spin on classic black-and-white dressing as she prepared for the start of Milan Fashion Week.
A beauty look made for the gown:
Lopez kept the glamour going above the neckline. Her caramel-highlighted hair was worn long and loose in polished, cascading waves, with plenty of volume through the lengths. Rather than competing with the elaborate dress and necklace, the style added to the romantic quality of the ensemble.
Her makeup similarly leaned into her signature glow. Lopez appeared to wear luminous skin, sculpted bronzed cheeks, defined eyes with fluttery lashes and a glossy pink lip. The warm tones softened the drama of the black gown while allowing the colorful necklace to remain one of the outfit's biggest focal points.
The glamorous appearance comes just two months after Lopez reunited with Dolce & Gabbana for the Italian house's Alta Moda celebrations in Sicily. Speaking to Vogue at the July event, Lopez explained how transformative fashion can be for her, particularly when she wears the Italian label.
She said the designers' clothes can make her feel "like a queen for a night," while describing the way clothing allows her to step into a different character.
Her latest Milan look certainly seemed to channel that same philosophy.
Milan Fashion Week officially kicked off September 22 and runs through September 28, with some of Italy's biggest fashion houses unveiling their Spring/Summer 2027 collections.
And if Lopez's first day in the city is any indication, her off-runway wardrobe may prove just as theatrical as the clothes appearing on the catwalks.

articles.title_orig: How investigators build a criminal case from drug overdose deaths like Hayden Panettiere’s
articles.title_zh: How investigators build a criminal case from drug overdose deaths like Hayden Panettiere’s
articles.content_orig:
The death of Hayden Panettiere last month is now the subject of a federal investigation into whether the actress obtained illicit and possibly counterfeit drugs from a dealer in Southern California, a source familiar with the investigation told CNN.
But building a criminal case from her accidental overdose death will be an uphill challenge for investigators.
Tens of thousands of people die from drug overdose deaths every year, but only a few hundred per year lead to criminal charges. Some celebrity deaths in recent years, notably those of “Friends” actor Matthew Perry and rapper Mac Miller, have led to charges. Others, like the death of the musician Prince, did not.
“These are just really difficult cases, regardless of if you’re a celebrity or if you’re just John Q. Public,” said Thaddeus Johnson, a former law enforcement official in Tennessee and senior fellow at the Council on Criminal Justice think tank.
The challenge for investigators lies in the gritty details. To make the case, they have to follow the trail of evidence, such as phone records, drugs and witnesses, to identify a dealer or supplier. Investigators also have to prove with toxicology, forensic pathology, and medical analysis that the specific drugs caused the victim’s death.
“Every case is different,” said CNN senior legal analyst Elie Honig, a former prosecutor. “Sometimes you can make a link. Sometimes you can’t.”
These investigations require significant resources, but overdose deaths are often not prioritized by police in the same way as a fatal shooting. Celebrity deaths may be an exception, though.
“It does seem that police are more attentive to and more invested in cases that get a lot of attention when it’s a well-known person who overdoses,” Honig said.
The challenges of bringing these cases are newly relevant as investigators dig into Panettiere’s death.
Panettiere, who wrote in a memoir of her struggles with drug and alcohol addiction, was found in cardiac arrest at an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16. Medics responded to the scene but were unable to resuscitate her.
Dispatch audio obtained from Broadcastify.com references a possible overdose. The coroner’s office ruled Tuesday she died of toxic effects of fentanyl and other substances, and the manner of death was ruled an accident.
Last week, US Attorney General Todd Blanche said bringing criminal cases in overdose deaths is a “big emphasis” of the DEA and prosecutors around the country.
“There’s a federal statute that allows us to go after – assuming we can prove who the dealer is – to go after them and put them in prison for murder. And we do it in every district in this country,” he said.
“So when we can prove – and sometimes if somebody is an addict, it’s difficult to prove who they actually got the pill from – but in the cases where we know who the dealer was, and we can prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the person sold the death pill to the victim who then dies, that’s a federal crime and that’s something that we will readily prosecute as often as we can.”
Why criminal charges are rare
While the US sees tens of thousands of overdose deaths every year, criminal charges stemming from an overdose death are rare.
There were about 79,384 drug overdose deaths in the US in 2024, according to CDC data. That was a sharp decline from the previous few years, when more than 100,000 people died of drug overdoses.
By comparison, a total of 1,340 people were sentenced for a federal drug trafficking offense involving a drug overdose between fiscal years 2019 to 2023, according to a 2025 report from the US Sentencing Commission. That works out to about 270 cases per year.
About 95% of the cases involved fentanyl, a synthetic fentanyl analog or heroin, the commission’s report found. Most of the people selling or using drugs did not know the exact drugs involved, the report states.
More than 8,000 defendants were convicted of fentanyl-related offenses from January 2025 to September 2026, double the number of convictions from the period four years earlier, according to a Department of Justice official.
“These numbers are proof that the Trump administration’s relentless strategy to dismantle fentanyl networks and save lives is working,” a DOJ spokesperson said.
Building a criminal case out of a drug overdose requires two key things: Evidence of the drug’s source, and evidence the drug caused death.
For the first part, investigators use phone records, bank records, witnesses and other evidence to try to work their way up the chain to identify the dealer or supplier. But that can be difficult in the underground drug economy, as counterfeit pills may come from the streets or even strangers on the internet.
“Sometimes you’re chasing a ghost,” Honig said. “Sometimes you just can’t figure out where the end user got the drugs from, and once the chain goes cold, that’s it.”
The second challenge is proving that the specific drugs caused the death. The National Association of Attorneys General calls this the “lynchpin” of the case, saying “causation raises perhaps the most difficult issues in proving these cases.”
The challenge is that addicts may take many different substances, or they may be in bad health generally. This all means that the toxicology report and the medical examiner’s review is paramount in an overdose death, and those take time and resources.
“These damn cases are just so damn difficult to prove,” Johnson said. “You have to prove somebody sold the drugs. You have to prove that the drugs they sold caused the particular death. Those are different things.”
From Prince to Perry to Panettiere
Though criminal overdose cases are rare, a few high-profile deaths have resulted in charges.
On October 28, 2023, Perry, the “Friends” star, was found floating face down in his hot tub at his home in Pacific Palisades, California. The Los Angeles Medical Examiner’s Office listed the cause of death as “acute effects of ketamine” and subsequent drowning.
Five people later pleaded guilty to federal drug charges resulting from his death. The defendants were identified as a woman referred to by authorities as the “Ketamine Queen,” two doctors, Perry’s live-in personal assistant and a middle-man.
The evidence against Jasveen Singh, the so-called Ketamine Queen, included text messages, phone records and the discovery of drugs in her residence during a raid, according to federal prosecutors.
Similarly, the September 2018 death of rapper Mac Miller was determined to be an accidental overdose of fentanyl, cocaine and alcohol. Prosecutors later brought charges against men who allegedly provided the rapper counterfeit oxycodone pills containing fentanyl two days before the overdose. Two men pleaded guilty and were sentenced to nearly 12 years and 17.5 years in prison, respectively, per court records.
On the other hand, there were no criminal charges filed after the April 2016 death of Prince. Authorities said there was “no reliable evidence” of who supplied the counterfeit fentanyl-laced Vicodin pills that killed him or how he obtained them.
None of the medications found in Prince’s home was prescribed to him, according to court documents. Some bottles of opioid painkillers in his home were prescribed to an associate, and other medications were found in vitamin bottles and envelopes, search warrants showed.
In Panettiere’s case, after police responded to an emergency call when she was unresponsive, her boyfriend showed an officer a bag of her medications, according to a police report.
The coroner’s office report identified her cause of death as toxic effects of fentanyl, the synthetic opioid; 4-ANPP, a chemical used to make fentanyl; Alprazolam, a benzodiazepine commonly used to treat anxiety; Methocarbamol, a muscle relaxant; and Quetiapine, an antipsychotic drug.
Ultimately, the goal of bringing these cases is to try to crack down on organized crime and deter others from illegally distributing dangerous drugs.

articles.title_orig: These 3 Major Upgrades Could Be Heading to Your Next Flagship Android Phone
articles.title_zh: These 3 Major Upgrades Could Be Heading to Your Next Flagship Android Phone
articles.content_orig:
The year’s not nearly over, but 2026 has already delivered a glut of exciting Android phones. Still, we can’t help but think about what might come next. Every phone-maker has distinct ideas about what features they’d like to add and improve with every generation. Some of these things, like design, they can do alone, but others require close collaboration with their partners.
Two such partners are Google and Qualcomm – the former on the software side and the latter on the hardware side. Every summer at Google I/O, we learn about a slew of new software features that will enhance existing and upcoming Android phones. Then, every fall, Qualcomm, which makes the chips, gives us a glimpse of what power and features those companies, like Samsung and Motorola, will have to play with in upcoming releases.
On Tuesday at the Snapdragon Summit in Hawaii, Qualcomm announced a pair of powerful new chips – the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.
“We’re just now at the beginning of the agentic age, and Snapdragon is the platform built for it,” added Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, in his Snapdragon Summit keynote.
Of the new dual chips, it’s the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 that will really take phones to the next level of performance and AI capabilities. The chip “represents the pinnacle of Snapdragon innovation, purpose-built for the most advanced AI workloads and the experiences that will define the agentic era,” said Qualcomm product marketing manager Charlie Beeman in a briefing ahead of the announcement.
The Extreme sees inevitable improvements to speed, connectivity and efficiency, but more interesting are the tweaks Qualcomm has made to enable new experiences and features that it simply wasn’t possible to include on prior Android phones.
“It brings an enormous amount of compute power to a smartphone, and therefore opens up a lot of new opportunities in terms of the applications that could be developed,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS. “But it’s a bit of a chicken and egg situation because until that’s enabled on the phones, we won’t know what those applications are going to be.”
A question mark lingers over how different phone-makers will tap the power of the Elite Extreme, but Qualcomm has given us some distinct areas where we can expect to see new experiences. Here are three to look out for and look forward to.
“How’s the camera?” is pretty much the first question everyone will ask when coming across a new smartphone in the wild. Phone-makers know that image quality and camera capabilities are priorities for any new device, and while a lot of that comes down to choices made by the manufacturer, Qualcomm chips still run the show when it comes to the phone’s imaging pipeline.
Both of the new Snapdragon chips will enable a refined camera experience with intelligent stabilization and every pixel now carrying 16 bits of data. The image signaling processor is also tightly coupled to the NPU, a specialized chip that accelerates AI and machine learning tasks. This will enable AI to work on an image while it’s being captured, instead of after. This allows for a dramatic leap in raw throughput and professional-grade video, and a far deeper understanding of every pixel in your scene.
“Each element of the scene is processed individually, helping ensure every shot looks natural, consistent, and remarkably true to life,” said Lekha Motiwala, Qualcomm’s senior director of product management, speaking at Snapdragon Summit.
And the Extreme version of the chip offers more capabilities, such as enabling phone cameras to record video in 8K resolution at 60 fps or film in 4K resolution at 240 fps for super-slow-mo footage.
“You’ll see this coming for the first time in Snapdragon-powered smartphones,” said Motiwala. “It’s not just about getting a shot. It’s about preserving a moment as you experienced it.”
There’s simply no way for AI to be personal without it really getting to know you. Agentic AI that lacks personal context – past, present and future – would be like speaking with a different stranger each time you pick up your phone.
The 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is engineered to collect that context, hold onto it and draw from it whenever needed. This is all thanks to Qualcomm’s new Sensing Hub, which, with its dual micro-NPUs, can support models up to 200 million parameters. The company’s updated Personal Scribe can then remember who said what, why it matters and learn from your messages, emails and conversations to build your private knowledge graph.
It could expand an AI agent’s ability to give you nuanced answers to questions, help you recall when and to whom you made specific promises, and make future plans for you based on a whole range of factors, such as your availability, schedule, travel preferences and need for relaxation or concentrated working time.
With its ability to run over 30 billion different models on device, the Elite Extreme Gen 6 is definitely leading the way when it comes to running agentic AI. “When you have this level of capability, your work starts before you even open your inbox,” said Amon. “Here, an agent digests your [Snapdragon] Summit invitation, understands the dates, the flights, the venue details, key moments inside it, and it builds a plan.”
Phones can be overlooked as gaming devices, but for Qualcomm, providing a best-in-class mobile gaming experience remains a priority.
With the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 2, the company is introducing an AI-rendering technology called Adreno Neural Fusion, which is supported across major game engines, including Unreal, Unity and Messiah. It can deliver upscaled images with “rock-solid frame rates” at lower power, according to Matthew Grossman, manager of product marketing at Qualcomm.
Adreno Neural Fusion is “a proprietary technology designed by Qualcomm from the ground up, not an off-the-shelf implementation,” said Chris Patrick, Qualcomm’s SVP and general manager of handsets. “It’s a tightly integrated architecture that brings graphics and AI together to knock a new class of intelligent gaming experiences.”
In addition, AI-dedicated Adreno matrix cores run advanced models, and the chip features 18MB of high-performance memory. So what does this mean for your mobile gaming experience? The answer is better picture quality, higher frame rates and longer play times with games drawing less power than in the past. It’s a win-win-win.

articles.title_orig: E.U. drops sanctions on two of Russia’s richest oligarchs despite Kyiv’s outcry
articles.title_zh: E.U. drops sanctions on two of Russia’s richest oligarchs despite Kyiv’s outcry
articles.content_orig:
The EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war on Ukraine for the next three years.
With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve the Russia blacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously.
France stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan.
Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets.
The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests.
Ukraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.”
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added.
In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six.
A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”
A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution.
Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.
Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.
