articles.title_orig: Gable Steveson breaks silence after stunning UFC 331 loss, addresses 2019 allegations in lengthy statement
articles.title_zh: Gable Steveson breaks silence after stunning UFC 331 loss, addresses 2019 allegations in lengthy statement
articles.content_orig:
Gable Steveson has broken his silence following the stunning first loss of his professional MMA career.
Steveson released a lengthy statement Tuesday through his manager, Abraham Kawa, addressing his historic 12-second upset at the hands of Sean Sharaf at UFC 331. The Olympic champion described the defeat as a "mistake on my end" and vowed to respond much like he did following setbacks during his decorated amateur wrestling career.
"Just like my wrestling days after my loss, I came back with an undeniable will to win and focus that led me to the top of my sport. The result of Saturday night, I believe, will catapult me to do the same," Steveson wrote. "I will be great, and this won't deny me."
Steveson also addressed the allegations of sexual assault stemming from a 2019 incident in his college years that resurfaced during UFC 331 fight week.
Steveson's full statement can be read below:
— Abe kawa (@Abraham_kawa) September 22, 2026
This statement is for my family, my friends, my fans, and the people who truly know me and know the kind of man I am. I know there are people who will never support me, no matter what I say or do. That's their choice. But I'm speaking to the people who know me, not just as an athlete, but as a husband and a father to a young daughter.
Prior to and during fight week, an incident from my college years was brought up by my opponent. I believe it was raised to get in my head, but it also reopened something that had been addressed years ago.
I want to be clear: I did not do anything alleged. I was never charged with a crime, and the matter was ultimately dropped by the district attorney. The allegations were not ignored nor brushed aside. They were thoroughly and heavily reviewed as I fully cooperated with law enforcement, including a separate Title IX review.
There were no criminal charges, no conviction, and no finding of responsibility against me. The matter was closed, and there is no pending legal issue involving me. My own attorney did their own investigation and stated on the record that even if the law was changed, I would have the same outcome, which now speaks for itself.
I understand how serious allegations like this are, and I understand that people may have questions when they hear only part of a story. Moving forward, I am going to keep focusing on my wife, my daughter, my family, and the work in front of me. To the people who support me, thank you. I know who I am. My family knows who I am. The people who have walked with me through life know who I am. That's what matters to me, and that's where I'm going to keep my focus.
As for my opponent, congratulations. You caught me. A mistake on my end was made. It was your night. Just like my wrestling days after my loss, I came back with an undeniable will to win and focus that led me to the top of my sport. The result of Saturday night, I believe, will catapult me to do the same. I will be great, and this won't deny me.
Steveson, 26, entered UFC 331 with many hailing him as the most talented heavyweight prospect in recent MMA history. His stunning loss to Sharaf, who held an 0-2 UFC record prior to Saturday night, marked the biggest UFC betting upset of all time for Draft Kings.
Along with being a two-time NCAA Division I national champion as an amateur wrestler and two-time Dan Hodge Trophy winner — the award given annually to collegiate athletics' top freestyle wrestler — Steveson was best known within the wrestling world for his run through the 2020 Olympics, when he stunned the global field at just 21 years old to become the youngest freestyle wrestler in his division to ever win gold.
Entering UFC 331, Steveson was already 4-0 with four first-round knockouts in his first year as a professional MMA fighter, culminating in a two-minute thrashing of Elisha Ellison this past July in his UFC debut. His matchup with Sharaf, however, proved to be different in more ways than one, as the former U.S. Marine made Steveson's 2019 sexual assault allegations a central focus of the bout's pre-fight build.
In June 2019, Steveson and a teammate on the University of Minnesota wrestling team, Dylan Martinez, were arrested on suspicion of sexual assault. The case was ultimately dropped after investigators determined there was "inadequate evidence" to convict the two wrestlers. Prosecutors also pointed to a Minnesota law that limited how sexual assault cases involving intoxicated victims could be charged. That law has since been changed.
In the immediate aftermath of Steveson's loss at UFC 331, the heavyweight prospect fled the cage before the result's official announcement could be read — a decision which drew a flood of criticism. UFC Hall of Famer Daniel Cormier went so far as to lambaste the Olympian for being an "ungrateful loser" on UFC 331's post-fight broadcast.
UFC legend Jon Jones, who has served as one of Steveson's primary mentors and coaches, has since said it was his decision "to take Gable straight to the back after the fight," citing a desire to "get my friend to the back to make sure he was OK."

articles.title_orig: Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
articles.title_zh: Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
articles.content_orig:
Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
The EU Industry Commissioner warned that the EU will consider using punitive trade measures if Beijing does not rebalance the trade deficit, which costs the bloc thousands of jobs every week.
The European Union "urgently" needs to act quickly to rebalance its "unsustainable" trade relationship with China, Commission Executive Vice-President for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy, Stéphane Séjourné, told Euronews, stressing that significant job losses are at stake.
Recent customs data showed the gap between the bloc's imports from China and exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1 billion a day in July.
"This trade rebalancing is becoming existential for Europeans," Séjourné said on Euronews' interview programme The Europe Conversation.
"Today we're losing thousands of jobs every week," he noted, adding that the EU already lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year. These were particularly concentrated in energy-intensive sectors and automotive supply chains. "It's urgent that we act, and urgent that we rebalance."
The EU, meanwhile, began crucial negotiations with Beijing in June this year, and has set a looming October deadline for concrete, "credible" outcomes. This will culminate in a high-stakes visit by EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to Beijing on 8 and 9 October, where Brussels is hoping to secure commitments from China that it will curb exports to the EU.
"The European Commission has put forward a proposal to the Chinese side to discuss this sector by sector and look at how we can rebalance things," Séjourné said. "This imbalance isn't sustainable, not for China or for the EU."
However, so far, Beijing has been resisting calls from the Europeans, pushing back against calls for voluntary export curbs.
The EU Industry Commissioner said that negotiation and discussion will be "given a chance," but that the Commission has been clear on the consequences of talks not producing the results.
"Trade defence tools are on the table," he warned. "Today we need credibility in how we use these tools, and we won't hesitate to use them to rebalance things."
Tools currently on the table include anti-dumping duties and tariffs against unfair subsidies (in industries such as electric vehicles and solar panels).
But Brussels is walking a tightrope when it comes to defending the EU market, as Chinese retaliation could see the country restrict exports of rare earths, essential to several of the EU's key industries, including defence.
The EU will also be keeping its eye on talks between Washington and Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping is landing in the United States for a three-day summit with US President Donald Trump, which is set to cover issues ranging from trade to AI and rare earths.
The outcome of these talks between the two economic superpowers could directly affect Europe's economic interests, Séjourné explained.
"We need a constructive dialogue between China and the United States. As we saw last year, the trade escalation between Washington and Beijing on these issues could spark a trade war, one that could even affect the European economy."
Last year, an explosive tit-for-tat trade war saw the US and China hike tariffs on each other's goods to dizzying heights. At the peak of this battle, the US imposed 145% tariffs on Chinese imports, while Beijing's retaliatory duties reached 125%.
For Europe, a trade war between the US and China hits hard, as astronomical tariffs on China inevitably lead to the diversion of Chinese goods from the US to the EU.
On the agenda this week in the US will be the looming expiration of the trade truce, due to expire on 10 November.
"I hope this dialogue can be constructive, that an agreement can be reached, and that the situation can be stabilised," Séjourné concluded.

articles.title_orig: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China's lunar "exploration" plans
articles.title_zh: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China's lunar "exploration" plans
articles.content_orig:
In a forthcoming memoir, former US politician and NASA Administrator Bill Nelson offers a blistering assessment of China, saying the United States must do all it can to retain its leadership in space exploration.
“Beijing’s intended strategy is to dominate the high ground of the twenty-first century,” writes Nelson in Space Odyssey, a book to be published by Harper Horizon in January 2027.
A former Congressman and Senator from Florida, Nelson served as a mission specialist on a space shuttle flight in 1986 and later as NASA administrator from May 2021 to January 2025 under President Biden. The book largely focuses on his space policy work in Congress and his tenure as NASA’s leader.
Nelson recounts how in early 2023, NASA assisted the US military when a Chinese spy balloon began traversing the United States. With its experience in using balloons to map the stratosphere and model atmospheric currents, NASA provided information on how to shoot the balloon down without endangering anyone on the ground.
He argues that the balloon saga offered further affirmation that the United States was enmeshed in a high-stakes competition with China for the high ground.
“What many Americans first registered as a balloon violating our airspace was really a warning that the next great rivalry will not be fought on land or sea but the skies above us and even beyond our atmosphere,” he writes. “The episode was also a window into the new space race that is swiftly approaching its most urgent phase, with the stakes even higher than the Cold War contest.”
Nelson has long been wary of China as a threat to the United States, noting his concerns about technology theft from the West. Unlike his predecessor under a Democratic president—former astronaut Charlie Bolden, who served as NASA leader under President Obama—Nelson supported the Wolf Amendment, which strictly limits cooperation between NASA and China’s space program.

articles.title_orig: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.title_zh: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.content_orig:
America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
Long-standing educational programs such as Fulbright, Boren, and the Critical Language Scholarship are all suspended. A leader-level deal could bring them back and protect the students who take part.
- Rosie LevineExecutive Director of the U.S.-China Education Trust
- Rush DoshiCFR ExpertC.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia Studies and Director of the China Strategy Initiative
Derk Bodde set out for Beijing in 1948 expecting to spend a quiet year translating an esoteric work of Chinese philosophy. Instead, as the first recipient of the newly created Fulbright fellowship in China, he found himself an eyewitness to the Chinese Communist Party’s takeover, and his account of what he saw became a rare firsthand record for policymakers, academics, and the American public. When China closed to foreign contact for the next quarter-century, Bodde’s expertise didn’t just remain useful: it was irreplaceable.
Bodde’s story is a clear example of the ways in which in-country research is a proven and often indispensable tool to strengthen American expertise of foreign countries—and not only with friendly nations. But as Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping prepare to meet tomorrow in Washington, DC, only around two thousand Americans are studying in China, down from fifteen thousand a decade ago, and the public and private ecosystem that once supported deep American study of China is collapsing precisely when it is needed most.
That decline is due both to funding cuts and legitimate concerns that students may face risks of arbitrary detention in China. Currently, two American academics have been designated as wrongfully detained after traveling to China for academic purposes, creating risks that must be addressed by Beijing. Such cases are rare—the vast majority of Americans who study in China do so without incident—but they are real, and their chilling effect reaches far beyond the individuals involved. At the upcoming summit, Presidents Trump and President Xi should elevate specific programs like Fulbright into leader-level deliverables, with President Xi’s high-profile support for them at the summit providing implicit assurances that participants will not face undue risks from China’s security services.
This approach has some precedent. Exchange programs sometimes receive broad protections from leaders. Indeed, even at the height of the Cold War, the United States established the International Research and Exchanges Board (IREX) in 1968 as a formalized, bilateral academic exchange mechanism, sending generations of American Sovietologists into the Soviet Union, even as the two countries remained locked in rivalry. IREX and its successors, including the Committee on Scholarly Communication with the People’s Republic of China, which managed similar style exchanges with China before diplomatic normalization, were established to lend U.S. government protection to academic exchanges deemed essential to the national interest.
By contrast, the China programs that built a generation of expertise are now defunct. The Fulbright Program has been suspended in China since 2020, partly over risks that participating students and researchers might be detained by China. Alongside Fulbright, less well-known but essential U.S. government–funded programs specifically designed to encourage greater foreign area expertise in government have been suspended to mainland China, including the Boren Awards, the Critical Language Scholarship, the National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI-Y), and more.
At home, the area studies infrastructure in U.S. universities that was built in the 1950s, including the National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and Foreign Language and Area Studies (FLAS) fellowships, has been gutted amid cuts at the Department of Education. In recent weeks, new unclear federal restrictions on higher education’s ties to China have pushed some universities to conclude that even nonsensitive academic engagement—undergraduate study abroad included—carries too much risk: the University of North Carolina is the latest institution to pull down its study abroad program.
Critics of travel to China argue that Taiwan offers a safer alternative for Mandarin language study, and that the extent of state surveillance makes the risk of visiting China not worth the potential benefits. But Taiwan’s educational opportunities, while excellent, cannot fully substitute for the loss of access to China’s economy, society, and culture.
America needs a much deeper supply of China experts to handle a fast-changing relationship. In closed-door meetings compiled for the U.S.-China Education Trust’s 2026 report, America’s China Talent Challenge, stakeholders across the U.S. government, business, and academia described how their sectors depend on American expertise to interpret China’s actions—from geopolitics and security, to trade and supply chains—and to keep the United States competitive. The working group concluded that China expertise must be considered a national resource.
As Trump and Xi meet in Washington, progress on people-to-people diplomacy may be less challenging than in other domains. But both sides can take steps to improve the situation.
First, the Trump administration should negotiate with Beijing to elevate specific programs, from named legacy programs—including the Fulbright, Boren, Critical Language Scholarship, and NSLI-Y—to new initiatives, into summit deliverables. President Xi’s endorsement of these programs would provide implicit protection for those students who participate in them. President Trump could privately push to formalize assurances that participants will face no risks from China’s security services. And to make that gesture credible, Beijing should release detained academics.
Second, in tandem with these negotiations, the United States should reverse cuts to funding programs, which are in many cases entirely unrelated to China. The area studies infrastructure built nearly eighty years ago, to include National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and FLAS fellowships, has been gutted and should be restored. Congress should also fund new programs, purpose-built for today’s U.S.-China relationship. Scrutiny of university ties to China is in some cases warranted, but it should be scoped so that nonsensitive academic engagement, such as undergraduate study abroad and language programs, are able to proceed with appropriate safeguards.
To some, these proposals may seem unrealistic. But they are rooted in history and pragmatism. Washington has long had educational programs in countries with competitors and adversaries. Those programs were often sustained by leader-level understandings that they would be insulated from competitive dynamics in the relationship. Improving mutual understanding is inherently valuable. For both Washington and Beijing, it also reduces the risk of miscalculation. If the next generation of policymakers has no China experience, both countries will suffer.
A United States that no longer trains people who can read Chinese primary sources, sit in Chinese classrooms, or track policy implementation on the ground is hardly more secure and is substantially less capable. Rebuilding China expertise is not an act of goodwill toward Beijing. It is a hard-nosed investment in the United States’ atrophying ability to understand and compete with its most consequential rival.
The United States and China have few bright spots in the bilateral relationship, and fewer still that could be elevated into summit deliverables. Naming and insulating a handful of exchange programs from political and security pressures is in fact one of the most straightforward areas for cooperation that exists between the two countries.

articles.title_orig: US open to extending China trade truce, or bigger deal, Bessent says after meeting with He
articles.title_zh: US open to extending China trade truce, or bigger deal, Bessent says after meeting with He
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is open to discussing shared risks with China in upcoming AI talks this weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios.
Why it matters: The Trump administration has flatly rejected calls from industry to pace or slow down the development of AI, citing a fierce race against China.
Bessent's scheduled meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng could provide an opening for talks on U.S.-China AI safety cooperation.
"The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems. We expect our discussions to cover both open and closed weight models," Bessent said in a statement to Axios.
"Bessent and [United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer] are the point guys on China. So it makes sense the secretary is in this position," a senior administration official said.
Driving the news: There will be multi-hour meetings in New York City, focused on AI, trade, rare earths, and other economic issues, building on previous discussions held in cities around the world, sources familiar said.
The agenda will remain flexible to allow for substantive discussion across the range of relevant issues, sources added.
Possible working-level meetings will continue into Monday, sources said.
Catch up quick: Bessent has played a key role in the Trump administration's AI agenda.
He was among the few cabinet members who flanked President Trump during a G7 press conference in June, where top AI CEOs and the administration discussed a U.S.-led effort to coordinate global AI standards.
Bessent also helped cool Anthropic's relations with the administration following a fallout with the Pentagon and is viewed as a reasonable actor who is trusted by the private sector and critical infrastructure operators, sources familiar have previously told Axios.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick led high-profile AI discussions during the G20 summit in North Carolina earlier this month, while Bessent is taking the lead on talks with China.
The big picture: Bessent's meetings in New York come days before Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's summit in Washington on Sept. 24.
AI CEOs have been calling for U.S.-China coordination on safety standards.
"All parties should jointly promote the open and inclusive development of AI for good and for all," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said this week, while pushing back on U.S. AI companies' calls to slow down and warning against "fear-mongering."
The bottom line: While a major breakthrough in U.S.-China safety cooperation remains a tall order, Bessent's involvement signals room for engagement on AI between the competing countries.

articles.title_orig: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China | US foreign policy
articles.title_zh: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China | US foreign policy
articles.content_orig:
When Xi Jinping, China’s leader, touches down in Maryland on Wednesday, he will step out into the arms – perhaps a hug, if Donald Trump’s wishes come true – of a US president who has shown China more bonhomie than any of his recent predecessors.
The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics.
Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.”
One area in which Trump and Xi may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening.
In the past few weeks, the US has been beset by worries that AI is progressing too fast, but that the US must strive to defend its lead over China in the frontier technology – and Trump has pushed back hard against calls to slow its development. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said recently. “And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”
On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, concluded talks with the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng by proposing an AI safety mechanism to be established between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism appears to stop short of a major safety agreement.
Tuesday’s front page of the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese communist party (CCP), ran an article saying that the US and China should “make AI a new frontier for China-US cooperation” and “make good use of the intergovernmental dialogue mechanism on AI”.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war. “Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said.
Still, China does not agree with US assessments about the grave threat posed by its AI developments. China’s foreign ministry responded to an essay by Dario Amodei, the Anthropic chief executive, that called for Washington to impede Beijing’s progress, by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
China has already taken steps to mandate the labelling of AI-generated content, to restrict the ability of children to use AI companions and, in keeping with the CCP’s desire to keep tight control on all information, to restrict what can be said by chatbots.
China may be more concerned with what it sees as US attempts to limit is growth. Washington has for years restricted China’s ability to buy the most advanced semiconductors needed for AI development, and this year the US banned the sale of Chinese humanoid robots.
Amanda Hsiao, China director at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy, said: “China doesn’t necessarily see the threat in the same way that the US does. There is a lot of distrust that’s in the way of cooperation. The Chinese are inclined to think of every US call for safety standards or calls from companies for pacing the frontier as means of suppressing Chinese development.”
Next on the agenda will be trade. Washington and Beijing struck a temporary truce in the trade war last year at a summit in South Korea. That truce – which included a pause on tariffs, as well as an agreement for Beijing to loosen restrictions on the export of rare earths – will expire in November.
Beijing is hoping for a longer-term commitment to banish tariffs, which pose a threat to China’s export-driven economy. But reports suggest that the US is unwilling to agree to anything that would weaken its future bargaining power.
Glaser, of the German Marshall Fund, said: “The US side views this as leverage over China and ensuring that they can get deliveries of the rare earths and magnets that American companies need.”
China may not feel the need to negotiate, either. Despite the trade war, China’s exports have surged, and it is on track to reach a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running.
One aspect of the relationship that has shifted since May is the issue of Taiwan. After the Beijing summit, Xi secured a major concession from Trump, when he agreed to pause a $14bn package of US arms sales to Taiwan. US presidents have traditionally excluded the issue of arms sales to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, from the US-China relationship.
But Trump has described future weapons sales as a “very good negotiating chip”. The US is now reportedly considering delaying further sales until after the Apec and G20 summits later this year, where Trump and Xi are expected to meet again.
Tuesday’s People’s Daily article said that a stable China-US relationship would “bring more peace, prosperity, and progress to the world”. But for all the talk in Beijing of “strategic stability”, Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, notes that “this is not a G2” alliance of the world’s two dominant powers.
“They are finding a way to manage the bilateral relationship, but they are not whatsoever working together as co-stewards of the international order,” Kennedy wrote in a recent commentary.
China is Iran’s biggest oil buyer and trading partner. After Trump launched strikes against Iran in February, China reportedly put pressure on Tehran behind the scenes to come to the negotiating table. It also slashed oil imports by nearly one-quarter in the first six months of the war, limiting global inflation.
Da Wei, a professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, wrote in a recent essay that this reflected “a more confident China” that “did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran”. But Beijing has otherwise done little to resolve the crisis in the Middle East, which it sees as being a mess of Trump’s making.
Last month, Bessent announced an “economic D-day” against Iran and its enablers. The US treasury secretary subsequently claimed to have had “very good private discussions” with Chinese officials over ending the country’s economic ties with Iran.
When it comes to Ukraine, Beijing has shown unwavering support for Moscow since Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, launched his full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser on the US and China at the International Crisis Group, said: “The contrast between the world’s incumbent power and its principal challenger will be even sharper in Washington than it was in Beijing in May: while the former is mired once more in the Middle East and straining longstanding alliances, the latter is casting itself as a stabilizing counterweight and the leading champion of a more multipolar order.”
The lack of momentum on thorny geopolitical issues, combined with China’s emphasis on maintaining “strategic stability” above all else, means that few expect there to be major breakthroughs at this week’s summit.
Hsiao added: “It is going to be yet another summit that is high on positive vibes and relatively low ambition in terms of substance.”

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping appears to be leaving China's CEOs at home for his Washington trip
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping appears to be leaving China's CEOs at home for his Washington trip
articles.content_orig:
As recently as last week, Chinese President Xi Jinping was expected to arrive in Washington with a large delegation of Chinese CEOs, as President Trump touted a dealmaking atmosphere surrounding the two leaders' summit.
Now, Xi is scheduled to arrive this evening with a significantly smaller business delegation in tow, dampening expectations even as an array of US executives remains set to be on hand for the gathering.
Chinese state media announced Xi's departure for the US on Wednesday, noting only a small entourage that included family members and political aides.
The South China Morning Post reported that a lack of progress on deals had led to the paring back of the list from the Chinese side.
US industry leaders had been expecting a wide array of Chinese business leaders to be in attendance from electric car makers and agriculture companies.
A White House official didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. Trump's team previously confirmed Thursday's state dinner would include Sam Altman of OpenAI (OPAI.PVT), Jensen Huang of Nvidia (NVDA), and Elon Musk of Tesla (TSLA).
The summit is set to begin this evening, when Trump will travel to Joint Base Andrews to greet Xi when he arrives at 6 p.m. ET.
The tone shift around business deals comes as other policy areas like AI and trade are expected to see only small steps forward, and signs emerge that Trump is set to roll out the red carpet for the Chinese leader.
Close observers of US-China relations have noted that Xi did not do the same when Trump visited Beijing in May, sending a subordinate for Trump's arrival.
Some of the US CEOs set to attend this week's festivities, including Huang and Musk, traveled with Trump to Beijing earlier this year.
Members of both leaders' economic teams are set to be in attendance, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, who met in New York over the weekend.
Bessent left that meeting describing the talks as constructive and saying the US had proposed a new AI safety "notification mechanism" that could allow Bessent and He and other officials to communicate quickly in the event of an incident related to AI. But China has yet to publicly embrace the idea.
The lack of further progress on AI underscored the modest ambitions of this week's summit that might be high on pomp and circumstance but light on policy.
There is little expectation of the US or China agreeing to broader limits on AI, such as regulating frontier models. In fact, both sides have signaled that they are eager to race forward with the technology.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
articles.title_zh: Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
articles.content_orig:
Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
Trump lawyers say White House access is ‘a privilege, not a right’; CNN, Politico and MS Now to present case in court after president banned outlets from White House grounds
Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. Several outlets have declined to publish any images or video of the president so long as the three outlets are denied access to the White House. And the members of Trump’s standard TV pool – five channels, including CNN, who take turns traveling with the president, filming his daily activities, and distributing that footage – have ceased their duties.
Trump administration drafting up plans for 90-day embargo on diesel exports: report
The Trump administration is readying to launch a 90-day ban on diesel fuel exports from the United States, following mounting calls from his party to take action to bring down the fuel’s price ahead of the midterm elections, POLITICO reported Wednesday.
Several people with inside knowledge of the conversations told POLITICO (currently one of three outlets banned from the White House by Trump) that the plan has created a schism within pro- and anti-embargo camps in the administration. It’s also prompted furor from the oil and gas industry that has broadly supported the president.
One oil industry executive privy to the conversations told the outlet that Trump seemed intent on announcing a ban by the end of the week.
The price of fuel has weighed heavily on Republicans in the lead-up to the midterms, which will determine whether Trump’s party retains control of Congress for the second half of his term. Trump ran in 2024 in part on bringing down the price of gas, but the war he helped kick off between the US and Iran, and the closure of vital oil shipping arteries it prompted, has sent the cost of fuel skyrocketing.
Diesel, in particular, has become a sore spot. The fuel for everything from semi-trucks to tractors to heavy machinery, it has surged in price even more than standard gasoline, to more than $6.50 per gallon.
That’s prompted some Republicans, especially those representing farming-heavy states, to publicly call on the president to take drastic action to lower the price of diesel.
The pushback, POLITICO reports, is coming from oil and gas executives and administration officials who warn that the embargo could raise fuel prices in the long run.
Yesterday, Britain’s new prime minister Andy Burnham navigated his way through a first high-stakes meeting with DonaldTrump at the UN general assembly in New York. His aides were delighted with how the meeting went, as Trump praised the US-UK relationship and described Burnham as a “natural businessman”.
The anticipated sticking points – theChagos Islands, WestBank settlement sanctions and Ireland – appear not to have derailed the talks nor cast a shadow over the future relationship.
In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to the our policy editor in London, Kiran Stacey. You can also watch on YouTube.
'I am the code': Trump reportedly clashed with White House ballroom architect after dismissing safety concerns
The Washington Post (paywall) reports today that James McCrery II, the first architect on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m White House ballroom project, resigned after repeatedly clashing with the president, who dismissed his warnings that design features Trump was insisting on violated building safety codes.
McCrery withdrew from the project last October after warning Trump that a preliminary design he wanted “did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures”, according to the Post’s report, which cites two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by the paper.
The sources said Trump brushed off the architect’s concerns, and argued that no building codes apply to White House construction. “I am the code,” Trump reportedly said.
The Post previously reported that they had also clashed over the size of the ballroom. One document obtained by the paper features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, with a note that appears to be poking fun at McCrery’s concerns. “James,” it reads. “And you think we are big.”
Another note made in Sharpie makes clear Trump’s preference for Corinthian-style columns.
When approached by the Post, McCrery didn’t say why he stepped down. A White House official said it was “factually false and totally inaccurate” to suggest he left the project over issues with the code, and said he was a “valued member of the initial design team.”
Discussions about the safety issues continued for months after McCrery’s departure, according to White House records reviewed by the Post.
It is not clear from those records whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that took over McCrery’s firm’s role in the project late last year.
The ballroom project is – unusually – being overseen by the Executive Residence, rather than the General Services Administration or National Park Service. The small office is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public, the Post previously reported. Typically, it’s responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.
Rubio, in his press conference, also touched on the war in Iran at several points, including on the surprise negotiations that took place yesterday between Trump administration envoys and the Iran delegation.
“I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough,” Rubio said. “But at the same time I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.”
Little detail has been shared about what was discussed at that meetings, though Rubio framed the conversation as a continuation of the earlier back-and-forth between the two sides.
Rubio also notably insisted that Trump would be able to see through his campaign in Iran acting on his authority alone, even if Republicans lose control of Congress in November and if Democrats were to oppose the continuation of US operations against the country.
Rubio also briefly addressed Trump’s meeting with Delcy Rodriguez, the interim Venezuelan president, who last night posed for a friendly photo with Trump at a Manhattan hotel only miles from where her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was incarcerated.
“It was a short meeting, but it was a very important meeting,” Rubio said.

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.
In a victim impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".
Weinstein has already spent six years in prison while he has faced three trials in New York over rape and abuse allegations. He has a separate conviction for sex crimes in Los Angeles.
He was originally convicted and sentenced in the Miriam Haley case in 2020. But in 2024, New York's highest court overturned the conviction, ruling Weinstein did not get a fair trial. He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.
The 2020 trial heard testimony from three women: Haley, actress Jessica Mann, and model Kaja Sokola.
Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006, and a jury found him guilty on that charge.
"I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she told the BBC of her decision to testify.
But in that same trial, the jury found him not guilty of assaulting Sokola. No verdict was reached on an additional charge of rape related to Mann.

articles.title_zh: ‘Dammit, something has to happen’: White House preparing plan for 90-day diesel exports ban
articles.content_orig:
Diesel prices just hit a new record. Would a U.S. export ban bring relief?
Some Republican lawmakers are calling for a ban on U.S. diesel exports as a way to lower record-high prices. But energy experts warn the move could backfire and drive diesel prices even higher by worsening the global supply crunch.
Average diesel costs hit a record $6.53 a gallon on Tuesday, up 77% from a year ago, according to AAA data. Diesel is vital across the nation's agriculture, trucking and construction sectors, with the price surge especially painful for farmers and small businesses.
Many of the calls for a diesel export ban are coming from lawmakers in states with agriculture-rich economies. Iowa Republicans Sen. Chuck Grassley and Rep. Ashley Hinson are among those calling for American energy companies to be barred from selling diesel outside of the U.S., arguing that could help lower prices for Americans.
Tennessee Rep. Tim Burchett, a Republican, introduced two related bills on Sept. 17, one that would ban diesel exports through January 2027 and another that would trigger an export ban any time diesel hit a national average of $5 or more per gallon.
"W diesel $6.57 in Iowa why doesn't Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on ag products bc food prices were inflated. High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME," Grassley wrote in a Sept. 19 social media post.
President Trump on Tuesday said his administration is considering a diesel export ban as a way to lower costs for businesses and farmers, according to the New York Times.
"I've called for it," Mr. Trump said of a diesel export ban, the newspaper reported. "I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it."
Why a diesel export ban wouldn't ease prices
But experts say a proposed diesel export ban wouldn't ease prices because it misdiagnoses the problem. They note that the U.S. exports diesel because domestic refineries produce more of the fuel than the country consumes. But because diesel is traded on global markets, prices have surged due to production and shipping disruptions caused by the Iran war and the Ukraine-Russia war.
In July, Russia banned exports of diesel amid Ukraine's attacks on the country's production facilities, removing supply from an already tight international market. Russia typically produces about one in nine barrels of diesel worldwide, which means it is now effectively supplying none to the market, Patrick De Haan, a petroleum analyst at GasBuddy, told CBS News.
Meanwhile, barring U.S. refiners from selling diesel overseas could increase the global shortage, pushing diesel prices higher, he added.
An export ban "is very likely to backfire," De Haan said. "Most lawmakers think, 'Oh, hey, this sounds easy, let's just back up products in the United States,' but that doesn't put them in the place they need to be. It's just fraught with problems that haven't been thought out."
U.S. refineries produce about 5.3 million barrels of so-called distillates — the energy industry's term for fuels that include diesel, home heating oil and jet fuel — per day, while domestic demand absorbs about 3.6 million barrels per day for these products, according to De Haan.
Diesel prices have soared because of global shortages, even though U.S. production exceeds domestic demand. Because diesel trades internationally, American consumers and businesses pay prices shaped by those global dynamics, he explains.
A diesel export ban could also lead to unintended consequences for U.S. production, experts told CBS News. American refiners could respond by cutting output, putting more upward pressure on diesel prices, or even shifting to producing other types of fuel that they could legally sell outside the U.S.
"Refineries are just going to try and get around it — they have a business to run," De Haan said. "There will be shifts that happen whether refineries start producing something that's not quite fully refined and exporting that, or they could very easily switch over to more jet fuel production."
Domestic refineries would likely cut diesel production in response to an export ban, removing domestic supplies that the ban was supposed to protect, Tracy Shuchart, CEO of energy consulting firm Hilltower Resource Advisors, said in a Sept. 15 social media post.
Foreign buyers would likely cement new deals with non-U.S. diesel suppliers, potentially weakening domestic companies in the long term, she added.
So what could lower diesel prices?
Instead of an export ban, the U.S. could turn to other measures to ease diesel prices. De Haan said the Trump administration could extend an existing waiver of a law, the Jones Act, that requires goods shipped among U.S. ports to be carried on U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged and U.S.-crewed vessels. That waiver is set to expire on Nov. 15.
Another option would be to temporarily waive a federal rule that requires refiners and retailers to sell a certain amount of renewable fuel, mostly ethanol, a step De Haan said could lower fuel prices by about 10 cents to 20 cents a gallon.
"Aside from that, the only thing that the administration really can do is get the Strait reopened," he added, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, the vital Middle East waterway that, before the conflict with Iran, carried a fifth of global oil supply.
Separately, De Haan said that fears about diesel shortages in the U.S. are unfounded. Although a handful of gas stations may report being out of fuel at any given time, data from GasBuddy, a real-time tracking service, shows no diesel shortages.
"It's not abnormal for stations to run out of gasoline —premium, mid-grade, diesel — and there can be a lot of different reasons for that," he told CBS News. "On a daily basis, there's probably somewhere in the ballpark of 0.5% to 1% of stations that may temporarily run out."
Some stations may also opt to delay buying a new shipment of diesel, given the current high prices, hoping to see lower costs down the road, he added.

articles.title_zh: China's Xi will kick off his state visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
articles.content_orig:
The Latest: China’s Xi to kick off visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who’ll be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who'll be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House. Trump’s decision to greet Xi shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
Also, Trump’s AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops. But what hasn't been previously reported is the presence of a drone port a few hundred feet away, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, which is already quietly operational.
Taiwan is watching closely as Xi and Trump meet and hopes US will keep up its arms sales
As China’s Xi Jinping arrives in Washington to meet with President Trump, Taiwan expressed confidence that U.S. arms sales to the island that Beijing claims as its own will continue — despite China’s pressure.
China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
Still, the U.S. government and Congress have “repeatedly expressed support for Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities,” Taiwanese Defense Ministry spokesperson Maj. Gen. Chiao Fu-chun told reporters in the southern city of Tainan.
Trump says his ballroom will house a drone port. The Secret Service already has one next door
Trump’s AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops, ostensibly to protect the 18-acre complex and the nation’s capital.
A few hundred feet away, a drone port, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, is already quietly operational. Equipped with cameras and sensors to scope out potential threats from a bird’s-eye view, the small UAVs stand on alert in four gray weatherproof boxes until deployed at officers’ commands.
The agency is using a model known as “drone as first responder,” deploying speedy unarmed drones from outdoor stations to serve as flying cameras. That model has been adopted by hundreds of police agencies across the U.S., often powered by AI software to help dodge obstacles or track targets.
The existence of the surveillance drones on a Treasury Department building adjacent to the White House complex has not been previously reported, and could undercut Trump’s legal claims that the ballroom construction is necessary “to protect the White House and surrounding region from aerial attacks.”
Xi is en route to Washington
Xi has departed Beijing on Wednesday afternoon local time for a state visit to the U.S., China’s official news agency Xinhua said. Accompanying him on the visit are Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, China’s ruling Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, it said.
China’s Xi to kick off state visit to Washington with rare planeside welcome from Trump
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who will be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House.
Trump’s decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
The White House hasn't released many details about Wednesday’s greeting, but Trump is expected to participate in an arrival ceremony at the base with Xi and his wife. The salutation will kick off a three-day visit that’s expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump’s May visit to China.
But it’s also a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump’s war with Iran and China’s designs on Taiwan.

articles.title_orig: U.N. Live Updates: Iran’s President Accuses U.S. and Israel of Lawless Attacks After Trump Threatens to 'Annihilate' Iran
articles.title_zh: U.N. Live Updates: Iran’s President Accuses U.S. and Israel of Lawless Attacks After Trump Threatens to 'Annihilate' Iran
articles.content_orig:
• Iran president speaks: In his UN General Assembly address, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will never bend to US President Donald Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” A US delegate in the room walked out.
• Trump on Iran: The US president said yesterday that he faces a decision between annihilating Iran or making a deal to end the war. The US said delegations from both countries held talks on the sidelines through mediators.
• Zelensky gives remarks later: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said he was ready for trilateral talks with Russia and US to end the war in Ukraine, is also speaking today.
• Eyes on Venezuela: Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez will address UNGA more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, who is currently being held in a Brooklyn detention center. Trump met with her last night as Washington maintains political pressure on Venezuela to enact reforms.
Rubio says Putin invited to G20 summit in Miami
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to attend the G20 summit in Miami, Florida in December.
“We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” Rubio told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
If the Russian leader accepts the invitation it will be his first time attending the summit in-person since 2019, before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“If there’s another opportunity for them to meet and there’s a purpose behind the meeting, that would be good,” Rubio said of a possible meeting between Putin and US President Donald Trump.
Why the Strait of Hormuz remains a critical sticking point in the Iran war
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian brought up the Strait of Hormuz earlier in his speech to the UN General Assembly. Months after the US and Israel launched the war with Iran, the strait remains at the center of the conflict and the global energy crisis.
Talks between Persian Gulf diplomats and Iranian officials — which were set to discuss an Omani plan for reopening the waterway to tanker traffic — were postponed indefinitely earlier this month.
Why it’s so significant: There are few places more strategically important to the global economy than the waterway, located between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Before the war, around 20% of global oil production flowed through the strait.
The waterway is only about 24 miles across at its narrowest point. Bolstered by sea mines, missiles and miles of coastline, Iran has long had the upper hand for controlling the shipping lane.
The US initially underestimated Iran’s willingness to close the strait — a strategic error that Tehran has capitalized on by leveraging its ability to threaten commercial shipping and prolong the war.
The current state-of-play: Despite shipping traffic remaining depressed, US President Donald Trump has insisted the state of the waterway is acceptable for now. In recent weeks, more tankers have moved through the strait due to the US military clearing mines and escorting vessels through the passage.
But commercial ships still face the threat of Iranian attacks, and there are questions around how long the US military can credibly maintain its substantial commitment of ships and resources to the strait.
What happens next: Trump administration officials have privately indicated they want to refocus negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program and not reopening the strait, according to three sources familiar with the matter.
Iranian officials have signaled that they would be open to nuclear negotiations with the US — but only when the strait issue is resolved and the US lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, a regional source told CNN.
As a result, getting the ball rolling on a framework to reopen the waterway is likely a critical step to pave the way for talks on an overall end to the war.
CNN’s John Liu, Chris Isidore, Nadeen Ebrahim, Kylie Atwood, Zachary Cohen, Lauren Kent, Annette Choi and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.
Ahead of Zelensky's remarks at UNGA, catch up on the status of the war in Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky will speak at the UN General Assembly later today.
Get up to speed on what’s been happening on the ground as Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds past four and a half years, with no sign of stopping anytime soon:
- No letup with strikes: Russia continues to hit Kyiv and other cities throughout Ukraine with drones and missiles, as Ukraine has been hammering Russian fuel infrastructure for months. Today, Russia targeted warehouses in Odesa, areas of Kyiv and a Zaporizhzhia shopping center. Over the weekend, Ukraine carried out its largest-ever drone attack on the Russian capital and surrounding area as voting in parliamentary elections entered the final day. Earlier this month, a Russian drone hit a train near Ukraine’s border with Poland as a group of former Western officials traveled out of the country, and NATO countries on the alliance’s eastern flank remain on high alert.
- Trump claims agreement: US President Donald Trump last Tuesday said Ukraine and Russia agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy targets amid concerns over the global spike in fuel prices — but both Zelensky and the Kremlin later described it as a proposal rather than a firm agreement.
- Russian missile attacks: Russia has increasingly been launching high-speed missile attacks across Ukraine, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of US-made Patriot air defense interceptors. That shortage has been compounded by a global supply crunch due to the Iran war.
- Ukraine targets logistics hubs: Ukraine, meanwhile, has recently struck deep into Russian territory, sparking fuel shortages. Kyiv has also stepped up attacks on Ozon logistics hubs in Russia — a competitor to the frequently targeted e-commerce giant Wildberries — as it seeks to undermine Moscow’s war-driven economy.
- First visit from US envoys: Special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner pushed for a return to trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine in a meeting with top Ukrainian officials earlier this month, which marked their first trip to Kyiv since the war began. The talks followed intensive meetings between the US team and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Russia hit Kyiv a day after the visit.
CNN’s Laura Sharman, Svitlana Vlasova, Darya Tarasova, Ivana Kottasová, Sophie Tanno, Lex Harvey, Chris Isidore, Matt Egan, Nathan Hodge, Clare Sebastian, Zahra Ullah, Anna Chernova, Katharina Krebs, Kosta Gak, Sophie Tanno, Billy Stockwell and Victoria Butenko contributed reporting.
Rubio: 'No discussion' of extending US final withdrawal from Iraq
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there has been “no discussion” of extending the US’ final withdrawal from Iraq, which is slated for the end of this month.
The US military presence in Iraq is scheduled to officially end on September 30 after more than two decades, following a 2024 agreement to withdraw remaining troops after the end of the ISIS campaign.
Still, Baghdad has struggled to deal with the militias within its country. Iranian-backed militia in Iraq have launched waves of strikes on US and allied interests amid the war in Iran.
Rubio, who met with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi at the UN General Assembly on Monday, said al-Zaidi did not ask the US to extend its presence.
President Donald Trump also saw al-Zaidi “briefly” on Tuesday night, Rubio told reporters in New York.
Responding to a question from CNN, Rubio said the US has “zero doubt” of al-Zaidi’s commitment to try to control the Iraqi militias but noted that it is “a massive challenge.”

articles.title_zh: Sources: Jaxson Dart to have season-ending knee surgery
articles.content_orig:
Jaxson Dart is headed to knee surgery and that will end his chances of playing again during the 2026 NFL season.
Multiple reports say, and OutKick has confirmed, that Dart suffered not only MCL damage but also meniscus damage when he took a vicious hit early in the Monday Night Football game against the Los Angeles Rams.
Dart also sprained his PCL, but the torn MCL and torn meniscus are the major problems that must be addressed by surgery.

The only good news in this entire scenario is that Dart did not sustain any damage to his ACL. It is intact, a source said.
Dart and the Giants spent the past day or so seeking multiple medical opinions in search of options that might keep him from missing the entire rest of the season. Ultimately, because surgery is needed, the other options were eliminated.
Bottom line? Dart's timeline for returning to play following surgery to repair the MCL and meniscus is approximately six to nine months.
The New York Giants season has been derailed.
They won't say this. The roster is filled with good players, coach John Harbaugh is among the best in the NFL, and he has a very good staff.
But any NFL team that loses its starting quarterback is all but finished for the season. Yes, the Philadelphia Eagles lost starting quarterback Carson Wentz to injury and eventually won the Super Bowl during the 2017-18 season.
But Wentz was injured in Week 14. Nick Foles played only three-regular season games and then went on an improbable and outstanding playoff run.

The Giants face the next 15 games without their starting quarterback. They face those 15 regular-season game with Jameis Winston as their starting quarterback.
Winston has a 36-53 record in the 89 NFL games he has started. The Giants were 0-2 with him starting in place of Dart last season.
The Giants have had internal discussions on finding other quarterback options, according to a league source. But the chances of that conjuring a trade for a starting-caliber star are practically nil.
All ugly facts. But facts nonetheless.

articles.title_orig: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.title_zh: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.content_orig:
When the Milwaukee Bucks agreed to sign Gary Trent Jr. to a four-year, $64 million deal in July, red flags went up all around the league's office. Days later, reports emerged suggesting the NBA was looking into the signing, though details of the league's probe were scarce.
The league apparently found enough that it decided to launch a full-on investigation, according to The Athletic. The focus of that investigation: whether the Bucks used the contract as a way to circumvent the NBA salary cap.
The league reportedly hired law firm Hecker Fink to perform that investigation.
That particular accusation should sound familiar, as the league just wrapped an investigation on the Los Angeles Clippers and Kawhi Leonard that looked into the exact same thing. While both teams were accused of the same violation, their methods for allegedly circumventing the salary cap differ.
In the Clippers' case, the team was accused of using a team sponsor to funnel additional funds to Leonard as a way to get around NBA rules. Accusations surrounding the Bucks are far more straight forward.
The league is reportedly looking into whether the Bucks made handshake agreements with Trent to sign lesser deals the past two offseasons with the promise of Trent eventually receiving a much larger contract this offseason.
The issue stems from Trent's massive pay increase this offseason. After making $2.6 million with the Bucks in 2024 and $3.7 million in 2025, Trent's new deal will pay him an average of over $15 million the next four years.
That massive pay increase came after Trent experienced a down season, one in which he averaged just 8.1 points per game, his lowest scoring output since his rookie season.
When reached for comment by The Athletic, the NBA, Bucks and Trent's agency — Klutch Sports — all declined comment. Both the Bucks and Klutch are reportedly working with the NBA as it performs its investigation, per The Athletic.
Should the NBA determine the Bucks purposefully engaged in salary-cap circumvention, the team could see a similar punishment to the Clippers. The NBA came down hard on Los Angeles, docking the team five future first-round picks, fining and suspending team owner Steve Ballmer and fining Leonard.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s Pledges Multibillion-Dollar Investment to Help Franchisees
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s Pledges Multibillion-Dollar Investment to Help Franchisees
articles.content_orig:
McDonald's (MCD) has one final shot this year to supersize its stock price.
And that Hail Mary toss will happen in Chicago on Wednesday at a closely watched investor day.
"We think the Sep 23 Investor Day could prove a crucial clearing event in which management articulates a credible path to reaccelerating same-store sales in the 4Q/2027, protecting & growing operating margins (w/ potential SG&A leverage starting next year), and still accelerating unit growth despite the tough macro," Jefferies analyst Andy Barish wrote. "For the stock to rebound, management will have to convince investors the recent same-store sales slowdown is fixable (soon) and restore confidence in the long-term growth algo."
It has been a dreadful year for the Golden Arches — one punctuated by an 18% drop in the stock price.
Comparable sales for a resurgent Restaurant Brands International-owned (QSR) Burger King US rose 8.5% year over year, beating analyst expectations, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. The result trounced McDonald's US result, which reported a disappointing 0.8% comparable sales gain.
McDonald's entered the fall with a black eye, given the barrage of key initiatives it recently launched and plans to launch.
First, McDonald's debuted its new McValue menu by offering 10 items under $3.
It then launched six new drinks on May 6, with refreshers like Strawberry Watermelon and crafted sodas like Sprite Berry Blast. All the drinks are caffeinated and aimed at Gen Z consumers who have been going to the nearest Dutch Bros (BROS) or convenience store for a Celsius (CELH).
A nationwide Aug. 17 rollout of its Red Bull Dragonberry Energizer ensued.
But the revamped McValue platform, discounted breakfast offers, and broader push into specialty beverages all failed to generate the incremental traffic McDonald's was banking on in the second quarter.
Investors are hoping to hear a different tune tomorrow.
"While lower-income consumer trends and highly promotional QSR environment don't provide much support, we view strategic missteps as largely responsible for the recent slowdown in same-store sales/traffic, much or all of which can be addressed in the 4Q and '27 to reaccelerate trends," Barish wrote.
"We expect a relatively quick adjustment to the marketing and menu innovation calendars that drove execution issues in the summer as management and franchisees return to a workable balance (some digital promos returned Aug 10, Spicy Chicken McNuggets limited-time offer came back Sept. 1, Spongebob x One Piece promo starts 9/15)," Barish added. "Work around franchisee pricing and participation in promos and value offerings could take longer, we expect an update on convos w/ franchisees next week. Finally, growing awareness of the new premium bevs (Red Bull launched Aug 17), Rewards, digital/delivery, and EDAP provides at least a steady floor."

articles.title_orig: China ‘throwing gasoline on the fire’ in AI data centers race, say lawmakers
articles.title_zh: China ‘throwing gasoline on the fire’ in AI data centers race, say lawmakers
articles.content_orig:
FIRST ON FOX: As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping about the future of artificial intelligence, two top House Republicans are warning that the Chinese Communist Party is "throwing gasoline on the fire" by undermining America's effort to build out AI infrastructure.
In a new letter disclosed to Fox News Digital, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., and House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank Bisignano to determine whether money has been funneled from overseas through America’s charitable system to block the data centers needed for the U.S. to compete with China.
Specifically, they raised questions about hundreds of millions of dollars that American-born communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham pumped into nonprofits and organizations that are now among the leading organizations fighting data center development throughout the country. Recipients of Singham's largesse include the Party for Socialism and Liberation and the ANSWER Coalition, both self-described pro-China communist groups. Earlier this month, activists from both groups carried signs in a Chapel Hill, N.C., protest, merging anti-Trump sentiments with support for communist Cuba and opposition to data centers and AI development, including the message, "SHUT IT DOWN!"
"Under no circumstances can we allow an adversary, and our most serious competitor in AI infrastructure, to weaponize our own tax code and harm an emerging American industry," the lawmakers wrote in the letter, sent on Tuesday.
FROM AUSTIN TO NEW YORK, PRO-CHINA NETWORK FUELS WEEK OF ANTI-US PROTESTS AS XI MEETS TRUMP
The lawmakers allege that influence operations linked to China are exploiting tax-exempt organizations, nonprofit networks and social media campaigns to fuel opposition to the data centers needed to power America’s AI industry.
The lawmakers urged the agencies to investigate whether tax-exempt organizations connected to the network have operated for the "private or political benefit of foreign-aligned interests" and whether donor-advised funds and intermediary entities were used to "launder the origin of foreign-directed money into American advocacy."
A Fox News Digital investigation found that Singham funneled $285 million since 2017 to six U.S. nonprofits, including his wife Jodie Evans' group, CodePink, through two shell corporations and a donor-advised philanthropy fund run by Goldman Sachs, which said it closed the Singham account in 2024.
The nonprofits have functioned with tax-deductible status while actively involved in promoting communist regimes such as China, coordinating street protests and fomenting anti-American rage. They have denied being part of any foreign influence operation, and Singham hasn't responded to requests for comment.
Smith said China is helping fuel opposition to American artificial intelligence infrastructure by giving a base to Singham as he funds U.S. nonprofit groups involved in anti-data-center protests.
"This is the Chinese helping throw the gasoline on the fire," Smith told Fox News Digital. "The American people need to know that this is not just an organic movement."
Smith said Americans have legitimate concerns about data centers, including their effect on electricity costs and water usage. But he said foreign-backed organizations shouldn't be allowed to exploit those concerns to slow U.S. technological development.
Smith said that "the Chinese want to stall and slow down the advancement of AI in the United States because they want to win the AI war."
"Tax exempt is a privilege. It is not a right," Smith said. "We need to make sure that we’re not subsidizing tax dollars to help create hostility and unrest in our country."
Smith also called for greater transparency regarding the flow of money among organizations connected to Singham. He added that the broader issue extends beyond the tax code and could include questions about compliance with the Foreign Agents Registration Act violations. "Transparency is the biggest thing," he said.
PROBE INTO 'SUBVERSIVE' ANTI-AI SINGHAM NETWORK IS 'ENORMOUS,' FORMER TREASURY ADVISOR SAYS
Moolenaar said organizations presenting themselves as grassroots opposition groups are actually advancing the Chinese Communist Party’s agenda in the U.S. "Groups that portray themselves as grassroots are really more AstroTurf — very fake — being funded by entities that are working in partnership with the Chinese Communist Party," Moolenaar told Fox News Digital.
"The concern is that they are manipulating the messaging and opposition to different American investments, whether it’s data centers or other technological advances, trying to turn the American people against these technologies so that China would be able to have dominance in this area," he said.
Moolenaar pointed to the use of grassroots organizations, community groups, propaganda and online bots.
"We don’t want foreign entities of concern — countries that may be opposed to American interests — using our system against the American people and trying to manipulate them," Moolenaar said.
He said the lawmakers are seeking greater transparency into the organizations’ funding and tax-exempt status, including whether their political activity violates federal rules.
"When you see them actively speaking out against American interests and realize that groups like CodePink are aggressively funded by this network, that raises serious concerns," Moolenaar said.
The chairman said China’s influence efforts exploit the openness of American society.
"The Chinese Communist Party always has the goal of dividing Americans, manipulating and getting their propaganda out," he said. "They don’t have the freedoms that we enjoy, and they try to exploit our freedoms and use that against us."
China remains both a major trading partner and a strategic competitor, Moolenaar said, but the United States must avoid becoming dependent on Beijing.
"They are a serious adversary," he said. "They are a trading partner, which is true, and we need to have a relationship with them," Moolenaar said. "But at the same time, we do not want to be manipulated, we do not want to become more dependent, and we certainly do not want to be under their thumb."
The lawmakers noted that a bicameral group of congressional committees, including the Ways and Means Committee, the House Select Committee on the CCP and the Senate Intelligence Committee, has been examining how influence operations linked to the CCP allegedly exploit America’s tax-exempt sector to "sow discord and undermine our democracy."
"The CCP consistently identifies political issues under public debate in our country and seeks to corrupt those debates," Smith and Moolenaar wrote in their letter. The CCP, they added, seeks to "heighten divisions between Americans and to degrade our civic processes."
The lawmakers specifically pointed to opposition campaigns targeting the construction of data centers, which are critical to the nation’s AI infrastructure.
A June report from OpenAI identified two clusters of ChatGPT accounts likely originating in China that were used in covert influence operations targeting U.S. debates over AI and technology policy. One campaign, dubbed "Data Center Bandwagon," generated social media comments and images claiming that data-center construction was raising electricity prices for average families. OpenAI said it found no evidence that the operation achieved meaningful breakout beyond its own activity, but said it demonstrated how foreign operators can exploit existing local concerns to amplify distrust.
