articles.content_orig:
New Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Rumors on Cardinals WR Amid Struggles to Start 2026 NFL Season
Teams around the NFL are keeping an eye on wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr.'s status with the Arizona Cardinals, according to ESPN's Dan Graziano.
Graziano reported Wednesday that "execs around the league are wondering whether the Arizona Cardinals could explore trading" Harrison.
"Harrison is extension-eligible after this season, and as of now, the Cardinals would have a hard time paying him based on what he's shown in the league so far," Graziano reported. "It's worth watching out for a potential change-of-scenery deal in this case."
Underperforming Players With the Most to Prove 🏈
Contracts That Teams Already Regret 💸
Harrison, the No. 4 pick of the 2024 draft, is currently signed through the 2027 season with a 2028 club option on his rookie contract. He has made one catch for 33 yards through two games of his third NFL season.
Harrison was targeted twice in Week 2, although one target was erased due to a penalty and he made no receptions in the Cardinals' 31-7 loss to the visiting Seattle Seahawks.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said after Sundays's loss he didn't see Harrison's lack of production as connected to any issues with his effort level.
"The spots he was trying to get to, he was getting to, we just weren't able to connect," LaFleur said.
LaFleur continued, "I know it's like, 'Well, just get some easy completions to get going.' And that's fine. You also have Trey McBride, who's one of the best underneath guys in the world, and there's only about 60, 65 plays a game."
He added it was a "long season" and indicated he felt Harrison could see more usage in the future depending on the defensive scheme of the teams the Cardinals line up again.
McBride has gotten the largest target share among Jacoby Brissett's pass-catchers so far this season, hauling down 17 receptions on 23 targets for 136 yards and two touchdowns.
Among Cardinals receivers, most targets have gone to veteran wideout Kendrick Bourne and Michael Wilson Jr., the latter of which signed a three-year, $75 million extension with $47 million guaranteed earlier this month.
McBride signed his own extension last offseason, giving the Cardinals two long-term pass-catching options even if the franchise decides to move on from Harrison.
The Cardinals could potentially receive increase trade interest in Harrison should he see more usage ahead of the deadline. Whether the franchise will actually consider selling in November could depend on how LaFleur is able to help his team build on their 1-1 start, starting Sunday with a road game against the 2-0 San Francisco 49ers.

articles.title_orig: Trump faces Xi as strains with allies complicate U.S. pressure on China
articles.title_zh: Trump faces Xi as strains with allies complicate U.S. pressure on China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has spent years trying to squeeze China — imposing tariffs, cutting off access to advanced technology and pressing U.S. allies to reduce their dependence on Beijing. When he begins meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday, he'll juxtapose the long-standing bluster with the pomp and circumstance the leaders lavish on each other.
And the two-day tête-à-tête will take place as Trump confronts a China that has proved harder to isolate and allies increasingly reluctant to line up behind the U.S. to do it.
Part of that is Beijing's doing. China has deepened trade ties around the world while building leverage of its own, most notably through rare earths. Its global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year, reaching a record $1.2 trillion for 2025 even as its exports to the U.S. dropped.
But the shift also reflects Trump's approach. Since returning to office, fights over tariffs, defense spending and personal spats have strained relationships with traditional allies even as Trump has pursued a more transactional relationship with Xi.
Countries Washington has traditionally counted on to magnify its power are increasingly seeking room to maneuver between the world's two largest economies.
As a result, Trump enters Thursday's summit facing a test of whether strains with U.S. allies have made it harder to marshal American power against Xi.
"China is presenting itself to the world as the stable counterweight to an erratic and violent United States," said Ryan Hass, director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution think tank. "America retains unmatched power on the world stage, but leverage requires a united front and there are a shrinking number of countries willing to follow America's lead right now."
For decades, one of the U.S.'s biggest advantages over China has been its network of allies and partners. When the U.S. restricted technology or imposed sanctions, bringing major economies in Europe and Asia along made those measures harder for Beijing to evade.
China still lacks anything comparable: The Lowy Institute, an independent Australian foreign-policy think tank, scored the U.S. defense networks at 81.4 on a scale of 100, versus 18.9 for China in 2025. But Beijing does not need U.S. allies to switch sides to erode that advantage. It only needs them to become less willing to move with Washington, Hass and other China experts said.
"When democratic countries don't have public support for a counterpart, it raises the cost for leaders to align with the United States," Hass told CNBC. "It lowers the cost for leaders to defy the United States."
Trump has taken a sledgehammer to relationships with allies. He's clashed with NATO over defense spending, threatened to reduce the U.S. troop presence in much of Europe while announcing plans Tuesday to add troops in Greenland after threatening to take over the island and imposed tariffs on the U.S.'s northern neighbor Canada.
"Although our biggest economic complaints regarding China's economy are shared by many of our allies and partners, the current U.S. approach is to attack all of those countries ... instead of forming a common front," said Melanie Hart, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub.
Meanwhile, public confidence in the U.S. as a reliable partner has fallen. In Canada, the share of people who described the U.S. as a reliable partner fell from 83% in 2022 to 35% this year, according to Pew Research Center in June. In Germany, the share who said Washington considers other countries' interests when making foreign policy fell from 60% in 2023 to 23%.
Canada this month was invited to be the first "associate member" of the European Union as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government seeks deeper defense ties with Europe and less reliance on the U.S.
Foreign allies "worry that as soon as they make a deal with us, Washington will undercut them in some way that they will then regret," Hart told CNBC.
China has sought to capitalize on that opening, not necessarily by persuading countries to choose Beijing over Washington, but by making the choice less binary.
The country remains a U.S. security partner and a strategic competitor of China, with troops from both countries still deployed along their disputed Himalayan border. Yet Xi visited India this month for the first time in seven years as the two countries took what Tanvi Madan, a senior fellow at Brookings, called "baby steps" toward stabilizing relations.
Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion in 2025, according to Chinese data, and Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed to strengthen business and transport links despite unresolved security disputes.
"Uncertainty over Trump's approach to Beijing and strains in India's own relationship with the U.S. have given India another reason to keep relations with China on steadier ground," Madan told CNBC. "Even a tactical détente between the U.S., India and China can have downstream impacts on India's strategic environment."
The changing balance of leverage is most tangible in the economic relationship.
Trump's tariffs targeted China's reliance on U.S. buyers, while U.S. export controls targeted a deeper dependency: the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment Beijing needs to compete at the technological frontier.
Those pressure points remain. But Beijing has developed leverage of its own. China placed seven rare-earth elements under export controls last year, forcing companies to seek government approval to ship them abroad. China accounted for more than 70% of global rare-earth mining and more than 87% of refining and production in 2024, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
In short order, Ford halted Explorer production in Chicago for a week amid magnet shortages, while Japanese and European auto suppliers shut production lines awaiting materials.
Suddenly, the U.S. faced a version of the vulnerability it had spent years trying to create for Beijing: dependence on something the other side could withhold.
"One of China's primary objectives ahead of these meetings is to box the U.S. in diplomatically, to limit the Trump administration's range of action," Hart said, pointing to critical minerals as one tool Beijing has used.
That vulnerability now hangs over Thursday's summit. The current trade truce expires Nov. 10. Rare earths were again on the table in weekend talks between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
Bessent said Wednesday after another meeting with He that the U.S. was "fine with either continuing" the current truce or "examining [a] bigger deal."
Meanwhile, Trump has other cards to play.
U.S. and allied firms control critical parts of the advanced semiconductor ecosystem, and American restrictions limit China's access to its most sophisticated chips and manufacturing equipment. Trump has also allowed limited sales of Nvidia's H200 AI chips to China even as broader restrictions remain in place, making semiconductor access another bargaining point.
That bargaining dynamic is beginning to reach beyond trade.
A $14 billion U.S. arms package for Taiwan has been awaiting Trump's approval for months. After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was holding the package in abeyance and called it a "very good negotiating chip."
For Beijing, few issues carry higher stakes. China claims Taiwan as its sovereign territory and has never renounced the use of force to achieve unification. Xi also pressed Trump on U.S. arms sales and Taiwan during their May meeting.
The delayed arms deal has raised concern among U.S. allies in Asia that Trump could soften Washington's position on Taiwan in exchange for economic concessions from Xi.
But Hart said Beijing's objective goes beyond one arms package.
"Their bigger play will be getting him to feel like he has a deal with Xi Jinping underway" in which Trump believes he needs to hold back U.S. support for Taiwan

articles.title_orig: As the US and China race on AI, the Vatican presses for global safeguards
articles.title_zh: As the US and China race on AI, the Vatican presses for global safeguards
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump, right, participates in a welcome ceremony with China's President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People, May 14, 2026, in Beijing. (RNS/AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
On Friday Sept. 25, Pope Leo XIV is scheduled to give a keynote address at UNESCO headquarters in Paris, marking the first papal visit to the United Nations Educational and Scientific Organization in more than four decades, and capping off "a day of reflection on artificial intelligence, education and peace," according to the organization.
The pope’s visit to UNESCO comes on the heels of a Washington summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on Thursday, in which the two are expected to discuss, among issues of trade, the potential for shared AI guardrails between the U.S. and China.
Looming over the Trump-Xi summit are recent escalating demands for AI regulation — including from the leaders of top AI companies, who are calling for a global slowdown on AI development amid revelations of rogue AI agents and increasingly dire predictions that include civilizational annihilation. While Xi has publicly endorsed international cooperation on AI safeguards, Trump has resisted, dismissing the catastrophic warnings as a "hoax."
As the U.S. and China race for artificial intelligence supremacy, Pope Leo XIV has pressed both powers to accept international safeguards on the technology. Meanwhile, through formal diplomacy and a Catholic network reaching from Beijing and Washington to Silicon Valley and the Global South, the Vatican is quietly positioning itself as a moral convener in the AI debate and a potential bridge between the rival superpowers.
"Pope Leo could be instrumental in reviving the bilateral U.S.-China diplomatic engagement on AI safety," said John-Clark Levin, an artificial intelligence researcher at Yorktown and advocate for greater Vatican involvement in AI governance.
In his May encyclical on AI and the digital revolution, Magnifica Humanitas, Pope Leo offered the church’s teachings on human dignity and the pursuit of the common good to tech entrepreneurs and world leaders, while calling for stronger regulation and oversight of AI companies and models.
On Friday, Leo will take his appeal for AI regulation to UNESCO’s 194 member states, of which China is one. U.S. representatives will also be present despite the country’s plan to withdraw at the end of 2026.
"The voice of the pope is a powerful ally," for establishing international AI guardrails, said UNESCO spokesperson Matthieu Guével during a Sept. 7 press conference.
Though Vice President JD Vance once suggested Leo could help broker a U.S.- China pause in the AI arms race, calling it "one of the most profound and positive things" the pope could do for the world, Vance has since echoed Trump’s skepticism, questioning AI companies’ calls for regulation and urging them to police themselves.
But the pope’s formal address to UNESCO is only one of several recent Catholic diplomatic initiatives on AI.
On Monday, Archbishop Vincenzo Paglia, the former head of the Vatican’s think tank on life and bioethics, is speaking at the Gates Foundation’s Goalkeepers event on AI equity in New York City. In an August essay, Bill Gates said he was "fascinated" by Leo’s encyclical, and Paglia confirmed to Religion News Service that he had a two-hour private meeting with Bill Gates three months ago and plans to speak to him privately again during Monday’s event. Gates has already had meetings with President Trump and his team and said he hopes to meet Xi later this year.
He also pledged $1 billion to combat AI inequality in the Global South, an important issue for Pope Leo.
Bishop Oscar Cantú. (RNS/Video screen grab)
On Sept. 16, roughly 30 bishops of the U.S. episcopal conference held a two-and-a-half-hour private meeting with seven AI experts representing four technology companies. Bishop Oscar Cantú of San Jose, who was recently appointed to lead the U.S. bishops’ AI task force, said the tech leaders raised concerns ranging from job losses to uncontrollable models and sought the Church’s support for regulation amid resistance from the Trump administration.
"The value system of the Church and of the White House are not in sync, particularly in this regard," Cantú told RNS, adding that he hopes the White House will "think about not just the bottom line or our ego as Americans," but the common good of society.
In August, Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna of California, whose district includes major AI companies, co-led a bipartisan congressional delegation to the Vatican to discuss AI ethics, human dignity and national security. And, last week, more than a dozen bishops went to Capitol Hill to urge lawmakers to adopt AI safeguards. Cantú did not participate in the visit but said legislators needed to feel the support of both the American church and the Vatican for "regulation and legislation that makes sense."
"If anyone can," Cantú said, "the Vatican is well poised" to bring Washington and Beijing into talks over shared AI safeguards. Cantú said, however, that he was unaware of any current dialogue on AI between the Holy See and the White House.
The Vatican may find Beijing more receptive than Washington to its calls for AI oversight. China already imposes extensive domestic controls on AI and has called publicly for international cooperation, while the Trump administration has resisted comprehensive regulation.
Relations between the Holy See and China have historically been fraught. But despite Chinese government officials viewing the election of an American-born pope with concern, Leo’s public disagreements with Trump have reassured Beijing that the new pontiff is not a pawn in the U.S. administration’s pocket, said Michel Chambon, a Catholic theologian and anthropologist whose book, "Making Christ Present in China" examines Christian communities in the country.
But Chambon cautioned that China "will mobilize the Holy See only if it helps Beijing achieve broader goals — for instance, in dealing with Trump."
Direct Vatican mediation between Washington and Beijing may be "premature" to imagine, said Elisa Giunipero, a scholar of the Catholic Church in China. Nevertheless, she said, Beijing "certainly considers the Holy See a credible interlocutor" on international affairs.
Giunipero pointed to what she described as the surprisingly positive reception in China of Magnifica Humanitas. The Chinese and Vatican perspectives "seem to converge on the need to create global governance of AI," she said, with the goal of establishing "a broadly shared framework of rules at the international level."
At the World Artificial Intelligence Conference held in Shanghai this July, Xi said that "AI development should not be a solo performance by a single country, but a symphony of international cooperation."
China’s desire to extend its influence in the Global South and the Holy See’s efforts to include developing nations in shaping AI’s future may offer another source of common ground. At the event, Xi called for more equitable access to AI technologies for the Global South and promised to provide AI access and training for developing countries.
"If serious U.S.-China mediation is not feasible yet, Pope Leo can still shape conditions for future bilateral dialogue by efforts to convene the Global South on this issue," Levin said, adding that it could, "at the margins, shift the superpowers’ incentives toward coming to the table."
A Vatican-sponsored conference in Rome in September connected institutions in the North and South — especially Latin America and the United States — around labor, technology, inequality and the environmental transition. Participants said the Vatican wants to be a partner in ensuring the voices of people in developing countries are not silenced.

articles.title_orig: ICYMI: Budd Delivers Floor Speech Urging Trump Admin to Hold China Accountable for Targeting the Safety & Security of Americans
articles.title_zh: ICYMI: Budd Delivers Floor Speech Urging Trump Admin to Hold China Accountable for Targeting the Safety & Security of Americans
articles.content_orig:
ICYMI: Budd Delivers Floor Speech Urging Trump Admin to Hold China Accountable for Targeting the Safety & Security of Americans
“The CCP’s malign influence on the world stage is growing rapidly, and American citizens are paying the price.”
Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senator Ted Budd (R-N.C.) delivered remarks on the Senate floor yesterday ahead of President Trump’s meeting with President Xi Jinping of the People’s Republic of China. In his speech, Senator Budd called attention to China’s war on religious freedom, its role in fueling the U.S. drug epidemic, its relationship with key U.S. adversaries, and the consequential state of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) race.
Watch Senator Budd’s remarks:
Read Senator Budd’s remarks, as prepared for delivery:
This week, President Xi Jinping will visit the U.S. for bilateral meetings at a pivotal moment for U.S.-China relations. During his two terms in office, President Trump has been clear that under his leadership, the United States must engage with China given the reality of our economic relationship, but we can’t forget that China is also a competitor and an adversary.
The Chinese Communist Party’s malign influence on the world stage is growing rapidly, and American citizens are paying the price. America’s economy, our fundamental values, and our security—both at home and abroad—have been challenged by the CCP.
I’ve long believed a whole-of-government approach is necessary to address this, and I am grateful that President Donald Trump is at the helm for these crucial negotiations.
China is our most consequential geopolitical competitor, and we cannot afford to ignore the CCP’s ambitions to reorganize global order at the expense of the United States or underestimate the CCP’s rapidly progressing hard and soft power influence around the world to execute this goal.
When President Xi enters the White House later this week, I hope discussions between our two nations include America’s most fundamental values and responsibilities upfront: the protection of American citizens abroad and reiterating a zero-tolerance for violating the God-given right to religious freedom. Let me be clear: there is no excuse for the CCP to unjustly target American citizens abroad or their families, harass religious groups, or carry out a broad-sweeping war on faith in China.
To this day, eight leaders of Zion Church remain behind bars in China because of China’s attack on religious freedom. These detainments are egregious and cannot be ignored. China’s persecution of Christians and other religious groups must not go unaddressed. This is why, during my time in the Senate, I’ve sought to implement strict sanctions on any CCP official who is responsible for or directly carries out violations of religious freedom.
Under President Trump’s leadership, we have already proven to China that the United States has zero tolerance for religious persecution, and we have seen notable results.
At the U.S.-China Summit this past May, President Trump personally raised the case of Zion Church Pastor Ezra Jin with President Xi. Two months later, Pastor Jin was released and returned to U.S. soil, where he was reunited with his family after years of unjust detention. While we are deeply grateful for Pastor Jin’s return, we must never stop fighting to bring home the numerous pastors still unjustly detained and to defend the freedom to worship around the world.
China’s pattern of wrongfully detaining Americans, or relatives of American citizens, is not limited solely to religious crackdowns. I also want to highlight the bipartisan effort Senator Markey and I have taken to bring home both Dr. Youlin Chen and Mr. Min Zin, American academics currently being held in brutal and inhumane conditions.
I am grateful for this body’s bicameral, bipartisan support in condemning the People’s Republic of China’s repeated pattern of arbitrary or wrongful detention of United States citizens.
Here at home, China’s influence and key role in the illicit drug supply chain have resulted in the loss of far too many American lives, the destruction of families, and stolen livelihoods.
I’ve met with far too many families changed forever by the impacts of the drug epidemic. Through buying up American farmland, malign actors have brought the production of illegal hemp-derived products into our communities, and our children are paying the price. And by partnering with transnational criminal organizations, Chinese-connected companies have intentionally made highly addictive, intoxicating substances—like fentanyl and illicit vapes—readily accessible to Americans.
But make no mistake: China is aware of the consequences of its actions. That is exactly why Beijing has no problem extending law enforcement and counter-narcotics cooperation to other nations to mitigate these outcomes. But Chinese products are still flooding American markets in what looks more and more like a reverse Opium War. It needs to end.
Just last week, the Trump administration listed the PRC as one of 23 major drug-transit and producing countries. We have rightfully planted the flag, and now we must demand action to dismantle this criminal enterprise preying on the American people. Ahead of his meetings, President Trump is right to raise this issue directly with President Xi.
Mister President, the American people cannot be blind to China’s efforts to threaten our national security. Especially since the PRC’s growing economic and strategic relationships with adversaries like Russia, Iran, and North Korea have had sweeping consequences.
Earlier this year, at the U.S.-China summit in Beijing, President Trump and President Xi agreed that Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon, and the Strait of Hormuz must remain open for the free flow of global energy.
But if Beijing wants to maintain a productive relationship with Washington, it must recognize the consequences of continuing to partner with adversarial nations that fundamentally defy U.S. interests on the world stage.
Recent reports suggest that China provided Iran with intelligence, including satellite imagery that led to the death of three American service members.
A PRC State-owned firm has reportedly supplied Russia with materials for kamikaze drones, violating sanctions. And the PRC has reportedly supplied Iran with air defense equipment, among other goods, bypassing sanctions.
This behavior cannot continue.
America’s national security must remain at the center of every discussion shaping the future of U.S.-China relations, including the race to develop technologies that will define this century.
We are in a race with China to develop the next generation of advanced manufacturing technology, quantum computing, space travel and satellite technology, and perhaps most consequentially, artificial intelligence.
China’s cyber-threats to the U.S. government have been well documented and damaging to our government and private sector even before the rise of artificial intelligence.
The AI race is not simply about who builds the most powerful model. It is about who will set the standards, safeguards, and norms that will govern one of the most consequential technologies of our time.
Beijing’s national AI strategy calls for China to reach world-leading levels in artificial intelligence by 2030 and surpass the U.S. That reality should alarm us all—especially given that these models are being developed within fundamentally different political systems.
China is developing and deploying AI within its authoritarian system that employs censorship and state surveillance. In dramatic contrast, our models are being developed under constitutional principles that promote free speech, value individualism, and encourage private enterprise.
As the Senator from North Carolina, a state with a growing tech industry, thriving pharmaceutical manufacturing, a pivotal financial sector, and a critical agriculture industry, my state represents many of the successes the PRC aspires to.

In FocusPacing problem: can AI fears overcome US-China race dynamics and force a slowdown?
Despite US AI leaders’ warnings over the risks of rapid development, they remain locked in a high-stakes race against each other – and China
After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.
In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.
These public statements come ahead of a highly anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met in New York City on the weekend to discuss AI safety.

articles.title_orig: As NFL quarterbacks go down, here are some potential targets for teams in need - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: As NFL quarterbacks go down, here are some potential targets for teams in need - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Quarterback injuries have been the unfortunate story of the 2026 NFL season thus far. The loss of six starters from training camp through Week 2 overshadows on-field play for nearly one quarter of the league. Fortunately, many of the injuries are short-term issues with only a slight risk of derailing the campaign, but in a couple of cases, there is little reason for optimism.
The New York Giants might be in the worst position of any of the six teams that lost their starters. Jaxson Dart sustained a knee injury on "Monday Night Football" that, upon further testing, is more severe than the team initially feared. If any of the NFL's injured signal-callers are to miss the rest of the year, Dart is the most likely candidate.
If it is indeed a season-ender for Dart, the Giants' 2026 goals shift dramatically. For other teams, like the Seattle Seahawks, expectations remain largely unchanged even in the face of injury.
Here are reasonable expectations for all six teams with injured quarterbacks.
Injured player: Jaxson Dart (knee)
New expectations: Vie for another early draft pick
There is no sugar coating the Giants' outlook without Dart. What had all the makings of a (finally) exciting year is already down the tubes. The offense looked hapless with Jameis Winston on in relief against the Los Angeles Rams, and while the veteran has had decent stretches in the past, his diminished arm strength, persistent turnover problems and the immense downgrade in mobility he brings compared to Dart puts a firm ceiling on the Giants.
Winston will potentially man the offense for the remainder of the year after Dart's MRI revealed a worse injury than expected. In five games without Dart since his arrival as a first-round pick, the Giants are 0-5. That history suggests that so long as Winston is the man under center, New York will stand among the worst teams in the NFL. The silver lining is that the Giants should be able to add more premium young talent to their enticing core in the 2027 draft, but this was supposed to be a season in which that group elevated them out of the early draft pick range and into playoff contention.
Injured players: Caleb Williams (hamstring), Tyson Bagent (concussion)
New expectations: Fall into early-season hole, climb out when Williams returns
The hamstring issue that knocked Williams out of the Week 2 loss to the Minnesota Vikings initially looked like it would result in a long-term absence. Instead, the rising star is week-to-week and could even return as soon as Monday's battle with the Philadelphia Eagles. It would be aggressive to bring him back from a soft-tissue injury in such short order, though, and with Bagent suffering a concussion, there is a real chance the Bears roll out their No. 3 quarterback on "Monday Night Football." Case Keenum might make his first appearance since 2023.
If it ends up being no more than a one-game absence for Williams, the Bears will likely be 1-2 upon his return. The early-season losses might hold Chicago back from reaching its loftiest regular-season goals, but by no means would they dash the Bears' hopes of reaching the playoffs. The offense is electric enough with Williams in the lineup to rattle off a bunch of victories. Remember, this team started 0-2 a year ago and reached the divisional round of the playoffs.
Injured player: Jayden Daniels (dislocated elbow)
New expectations: Another losing season incoming
With two losses already on their ledger, the Commanders are in extreme danger of falling back into the NFL's bottom tier for a second consecutive season. It is difficult to foresee them stringing together wins with Daniels on the sideline, particularly because their next six games include matchups against the NFC West's top three teams and a rematch with the Eagles squad that defeated them in Week 1. Washington might have to attack that entire stretch with Marcus Mariota under center.
The dislocated elbow is the exact same injury Daniels sustained in Week 9 last year. He missed four weeks and reinjured the elbow in his return and sat out the remainder of the season. The recurring nature of this issue sounds alarms about Daniels' ability to stay on the field this year and beyond. And the rest of the team is not strong enough to stay afloat without him. The defense, for instance, ranks 27th in scoring through two games.
Injured player: Sam Darnold (glute)
New expectations: Contend for second consecutive Super Bowl
Drew Lock did just enough to lead the Seahawks to a season-opening win when thrust into action in the first quarter, and following a full week of preparation for the road opener at the Arizona Cardinals, he excelled with three touchdowns in a 31-7 win. Seattle should be in business for as long as it needs to roll out its backup.
Even better news for the Seahawks is that Sam Darnold might return to action this week. Coach Mike Macdonald said he anticipates Darnold suiting up for practice, and the extent of his participation will determine his availability for Sunday's matchup against the Commanders. Assuming the offense is back at full strength no later than Week 4, the Seahawks have a good chance of remaining undefeated in time for Darnold's return. They cannot ask for much more than that.
Injured player: Kyler Murray (concussion)
New expectations: Battle for NFC North title
The concussion Murray suffered in the first quarter of the season opener looked grim, but it will result in only a one-game absence. Murray cleared concussion protocol and will start in Week 3 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, coach Kevin O'Connell announced. Thanks to Carson Wentz and two solid performances, Murray inherits a 2-0 record for his return.
In a division where every other team is 1-1 and where the Bears have quarterback injuries, the Packers look flawed, and the Lions' defense is a mess, Minnesota has a chance to build a comfortable early-season cushion. None of the teams on their schedule until Week 9 made the playoffs in 2025. If Murray delivers the career resurgence the Vikings hoped he would when they signed him in free agency, he could lead them to a terrific first half of the season.
Injured player: Michael Penix Jr. (torn ACL), Tua Tagovailoa (oblique)
New expectations: Prevent disastrous season after 0-2 start
The Cooper Rush experience was dismal. Back-to-back losses and a 34-3 drubbing at the hands of a division rival made the Falcons look like one of the NFL's worst teams through two weeks. Help is on the way, though. Penix is cleared for action and will take over as the starter in Week 3, and Tagovailoa returned to full participation in practice, setting him up to assume backup duties. Health willing, Atlanta will not need to turn back to its No. 3 quarterback.
The problem is that Penix is not guaranteed to be an upgrade. He is 4-8 as a starter since his arrival in 2024 and has an immense injury history. He ought to be able to make better use of his elite offensive supporting cast than Rush, but it would require a breakout season from the third-year pro in order for the Falcons to erase their 0-2 start and finish the year above .500. And if things go sideways for Penix or he returns to the injury report, Tagovailoa carries the exact same shortcomings.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow off 125 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq fall as 10-year Treasury yield surges to highest since 2007 and oil prices rise
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow off 125 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq fall as 10-year Treasury yield surges to highest since 2007 and oil prices rise
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities fell on Wednesday as Treasury yields marched higher amid concerns among investors that more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve may be coming down the pike.
The S&P 500 dropped 0.6%, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 313 points, or 0.6%.
Declines in utilities, consumer discretionary and communication services stocks led the broader market's fall, with the three sectors shedding more than 1% each.
Equities were weighed down by an increase in Treasury yields, which jumped after the latest purchasing managers' index readings came in hot . The yield on the 10-year Treasury note reached 5.087%, its highest level since July 2007, while the 2-year Treasury note yield hit its highest level since June 2024 at 4.887%.
"We have a lot of strength in corporate earnings, but we also have this inflationary pressure, and there's a tug of war there," Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon, said to CNBC, adding that it's "not just oil" that's driving inflation.
"It's broader, and it's particularly in the services sector," he said. "There's no way that the Fed is going to lower rates or pause at this point. Probably we're going to see maybe two, three rate increases."
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday that "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to get inflation under control.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way," he said. "Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded."
Odds that the Fed would hike rates by a quarter percentage point in October stood above 73% following the developments, according to the CME FedWatch tool . That's up from 55.4% a day ago and just 8.8% one month ago.
Crude oil futures moved up as well. Brent crude futures for November delivery were last seen trading 3% higher at around $102 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up 2% at around $92 per barrel.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours during the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York. He described it as a "very good meeting."
Earlier Tuesday in his address to the U.N., Trump said he has a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
In Tuesday's session, the Nasdaq hit a new all-time intraday high and closed at a record, while the Dow finished lower. The S&P 500 was roughly flat, though the index is about 0.8% off from its all-time high.
McDonald's shares fell sharply Wednesday as the company unveiled a new multiyear growth plan alongside a warning from the company that high inflation and flat restaurant traffic are likely to persist.
CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC that the company is "not expecting things to change" as elevated costs and sluggish traffic continue to weigh on the industry.
Investors are not loving it: shares of McDonald's are down more than 5% in midday trading, on pace for their worst day since April 4, 2025 when they fell 5.7% and trading at their lowest levels since October 2022. The move extends a string of weakness: MCD is now on pace for its seventh straight weekly decline, which would mark its longest losing streak since August 2014.
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that activity on "mentions" contracts are "concerning."
The response comes after the CFTC informed some of its regulated entities on Tuesday that "mentions" contracts, where traders predict what one would say in a speech, televised event or earnings call, are susceptible to manipulation.
"I think a large number of these contracts have issues, and so we're going to take a hard approach in evaluating those," he said.
Selig also told CNBC the federal regulator has a zero tolerance policy on wash trading, after growing concerns that Kalshi has wash trading on its perpetual futures trades. The Wall Street Journal reported the CFTC is looking into the trades.
The chairman also touched on Kalshi's efforts to introduce margin trading to traders. Selig said the CFTC is evaluating the proposal and that it will allow only traders meeting "stringent eligibility criteria" to participate.
Treasury yields raced higher on Wednesday as new services and manufacturing sector data increased worry of further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
The 2-year Treasury note yield jumped 8 basis points to 4.464%. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield popped 7 basis points to 5.058%, a level not seen since July 2007. The 30-year Treasury yield gained more than 4 basis points to 5.347%.

Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday he expects the central bank will need to raise interest rates further to tame inflation.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way. Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded," he said in remarks for a housing conference in Chicago.
"In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," he added. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that."
Barr labeled last week's quarter percentage point rate hike "important action" for policy that was "out of position" in getting inflation back to the Fed's 2% target.
The remarks came as S&P Global reported that its flash readings on services and manufacturing hit their highest levels since 2021. Price pressures are also surged, posting their highest readings since October 2022.
The three major averages began Wednesday's session in the red.

Mortgage rates have climbed to a level not seen since 2024, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association.

Mortgage and refinance applications fell, while the share of applications for adjustable-rate mortgages rose. ARMs can carry a fixed rate for up to 10 years but then adjusts based on where the market is at that time.

Moreover, the fact that our decoder runs on a single CPU provides a practical path to commercial-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing," IonQ quantum research lead Nicolas Delfosse said in a statement.
AI drone maker Tekever on Wednesday said it had hit a $6.4 billion valuation, as Europe races to rearm amid the Ukraine war and mounting threats from Russia.
The Portuguese-British company, which raised a $580 million round, develops AI-powered autonomous systems including surveillance drones. Tekever says its drones have clocked more than 50,000 operational flight hours in Ukraine since 2022, when Russia's full-scale invasion began.
University of California Investments and Baillie Gifford led the round, with Merlyn Advisors, Crescent Cove, Ventura Capital and Iberis Capital also contributing.

articles.title_orig: Super-strong El Niño could lead to 450K deaths. Map shows the states hit hardest
articles.title_zh: Super-strong El Niño could lead to 450K deaths. Map shows the states hit hardest
articles.content_orig:
More than 450,000 people are projected to die from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño by February, according to estimates by climate scientists.
The toll is on top of the early deaths resulting from temperatures already driven up by the climate crisis. It will strike across the globe, from Indonesia to India, and Nigeria to the US. Many further deaths are expected from the droughts, wildfires and flooding that El Niños bring.
The heat deaths have been estimated at regional level, and the researchers said the projections therefore identified where measures to protect people could be put in place and save lives. Such actions could include better heat forecasts, cooling centres where people can shelter, increased staffing for medical facilities at the hottest times and protections for outdoor workers.
The El Niño currently heating up the planet burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon on Monday, several months before its expected peak. The heat is so much greater than previous events that scientists have called it “mind-blowing” and “Godzilla-level”. El Niños are natural climate events but may be made worse by global heating.
“The estimate of 451,000 people is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbours, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives,” said Prof Michael Greenstone, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and at the University of Chicago, who co-authored the report.
The estimate of deaths is for the period June 2026, as some heat deaths will have already occurred, to February 2027, which is when current temperature forecasts end. But elevated levels of heat deaths are expected to continue until June or July 2027.
The most affected countries in the next six months are the tropical nations of Nigeria, Indonesia, Sudan, India and Brazil. The US is in the top 20 most affected nations, with 3,500 projected additional heat deaths. More broadly, the Sahel region in Africa and south-east Asia are heavily affected.
The El Niño is also a “postcard from our future”, the researchers said, pushing up temperatures to the level the climate crisis is projected to deliver in 20 years’ time.
“Increasing emergency response and better targeting our efforts can save many lives this year,” said report co-author Dr Tamma Carleton at the University of California, Berkeley. “But 20 years from now, once today’s extreme temperatures become the new normal, we don’t want to be in a constant state of emergency.. We need to mobilise now to design, deploy and evaluate the tools that will save lives in the years ahead.”
The projections were made using peer-reviewed methods that track the month-by-month relationship between temperature and additional heat deaths in 24,378 regions across the world. This was combined with the forecasts for higher temperatures due to El Niño in the months ahead. The baseline was the number of heat deaths in the average month from 1996 to 2025.
“People have been able to forecast when there’s going to be shocks to crops, and give advance warning of that,” said Greenstone. “This new report is opening the door to being able to do it for an even more important outcome – I would say the most important outcome – which is death.” The report will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, but Greenstone said that, given the urgency of the situation, “it would have been irresponsible to sit on it”.
Food supplies will also be hit by El Niño, with the World Food Programme warning in August that its impacts were likely to push about 50 million people into acute hunger and drive prices up. A major El Niño in 1877-1878 led to more than 50m deaths due to drought and famine, with India, Brazil and China severely affected.
Prof Friederike Otto, at Imperial College London, told the Guardian on Monday: “The [current El Niño] event is a huge redistribution of energy in the climate system and is dangerous, because it is unfolding on top of a much warmer, human-influenced climate system.
“So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress. El Niño comes and goes, but as long as we continue to burn fossil fuels, it occurs on an increasingly hotter baseline, making it much more difficult for communities to deal with the consequences.”
The Guardian’s climate forum 2026: On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts—including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book tickets here or at guardian.live
This article was amended on 23 September 2026. Owing to information provided, an earlier version said that the figure for 450,000 projected extra deaths due to El Niño covers the period from September 2026 to February 2027. In fact it covers the period June 2026 to February 2027.

articles.title_orig: As NFL quarterbacks go down, here are some potential targets for teams in need
articles.title_zh: As NFL quarterbacks go down, here are some potential targets for teams in need
articles.content_orig:
As NFL quarterbacks go down, here are some potential targets for teams in need
The NFL season is only two weeks old, and yet six teams have already dealt with injuries to their starting quarterbacks.
The Falcons were already without Michael Penix Jr. because of his recovery from an ACL injury when Tua Tagovailoa went down with a back injury just days before the opener. In Week 1, the Seahawks lost Sam Darnold to a glute injury and Vikings starter Kyler Murray suffered a concussion. Week 2 was even worse: The Commanders lost Jayden Daniels to another dislocated elbow (the same one he dislocated last season), the Bears watched Caleb Williams get carted off with a hamstring injury and then placed backup Tyler Bagent in the concussion protocol, and the Giants saw Jaxson Dart go down with a knee injury whose severity is still to be determined.
The spate of early injuries to quarterbacks has reinforced the value of experienced (and reliable) backups. The teams that have them have remained competitive; Seattle and Minnesota are both 2-0 with respective backups Drew Lock and Carson Wentz filling in.
But the teams that lack a solid No. 2 or any real depth at the position have paid a price. Just look at Atlanta, where third-stringer Cooper Rush was benched during a blowout loss to the Panthers after throwing his fourth pick of the season. He was replaced by Jack Strand -- who promptly threw a pick-six.
There's good news in store for a few teams. Penix will start for the Falcons on Thursday night and Tagovailoa is back to fully participating in practice. Darnold is expected to return to practice in some capacity this week for the Seahawks and Murray has been cleared from the concussion protocol in Minnesota.
But that leaves three teams who could potentially be in search of reinforcement.
Case Keenum is the only other quarterback on the Bears' active roster and, although he has 66 starts in his 14-year NFL career, he hasn't played a regular-season snap since December 2023.
In Washington, it remains unclear how much time Daniels might miss. X-rays of Daniels' elbow were negative for any fractures, but coach Dan Quinn declined to provide any details about the MRI results. Daniels will not start Sunday against the Seahawks, but how long he'll be out thereafter is unknown. In the meantime, the Commanders will turn to Marcus Mariota, just as they have the last two seasons when Daniels has dealt with injuries. The difference this time around: Washington doesn't have an experienced third-string QB like they did in Josh Johnson last year. The team's current No. 3 is seventh-round rookie Athan Kaliakmanis, a young player who showed some promise in preseason but is still quite green.
The Giants are in a similar if not worse position. Dart could be out for the rest of the season, a much worse outcome than what was originally expected. Jameis Winston is expected to take over as the starter, but he's the only other quarterback on the Giants' active roster. Jake Haener, a fourth-round pick by the Saints in 2023, is on the practice squad.
So who might be available to help?
Finding a quality backup quarterback at this point in the season is difficult, but there are a number of veterans and young QBs who could serve as extra insurance, if not more, for teams in need. From potential trade candidates to street free agents and practice squad players, here are some players who may be under consideration, either now or after the next prominent starter goes down.
The sixth-year quarterback has seemingly found his groove in San Francisco as Brock Purdy's backup. After a standout rookie season with the Patriots in which he was named a Pro Bowl alternate, Jones cycled through multiple play callers and quickly regressed. He was traded to Jacksonville in 2024 and started seven of 10 games in relief of Trevor Lawrence. But it wasn't until he signed a two-year deal with the 49ers in 2025 that he really showed his worth as a reliable backup. He went 5-3 as a fill-in starter, recording a 69.6 completion percentage, averaging 7.4 yards per attempt and compiling a 97.4 passer rating -- all career bests. San Fran may want to hold onto him to spell Purdy, but it could also get a decent return from a desperate team for a player who is set to be a free agent after this season.
The 12-year veteran and two-time Super Bowl winner reportedly considered retirement in the offseason, but ultimately decided to keep his options open in the NFL. Garoppolo, 34, hasn't had any real playing time since the 2024 season, when he started the Rams' regular-season finale against the Seahawks, and he hasn't had any consistent playing time since the start of the 2023 season, with the Raiders. But he does have a 43-21 record as a starter, to go with a 67.4 career completion percentage and 97.7 passer rating.
Johnson, 40, is in his 19th season of professional football and still going, as a member of the Bengals' practice squad. He is the ultimate journeyman, playing for a record 14 NFL teams. Johnson was Washington's third-string quarterback last season until Daniels went down and he became the backup and then the starter late in the season when Mariota suffered a quad injury. His familiarity with offensive coordinator David Blough and Washington's other quarterbacks could make him a viable option if the Commanders seek outside reinforcement. But Johnson also has deep ties to Giants coach John Harbaugh (and his brother). Johnson had three stints with the Ravens when Harbaugh was their head coach, totaling seven games (one start) and completing 69.8 percent of his passes for 321 passing yards, two TDs, a pick and a 97.1 passer rating.
Levis signed to the Jets' practice squad on Tuesday, so should the Giants be interested in adding him to their active roster, he'd have a pretty easy move. But would they? The 2023 second-round pick by the Titans showed some promise when he took over for Ryan Tannehill as a rookie in 2023. But injuries and poor performances derailed his tenure in Tennessee. He was benched late in the 2024 season, when Giants quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan was Tennessee's head coach. Levis missed all of 2025 because of a shoulder injury and was released last month after losing the backup job to Mitchell Trubisky.
Richardson never developed into the franchise quarterback the Colts hoped he'd be when they drafted him fourth overall in 2023. Injuries, performance issues and general readiness questions after he tapped out for a play during a narrow loss to the Texans in '24 put him on the outs with the organization. He lost his starting job to Daniel Jones, requested a trade and is now in the final year of his rookie contract (the Colts declined his fifth-year option). If Richardson is viewed as more of a developmental project, then a team in need of immediate help may be unlikely to trade for him. But never say never.
The same context holds for McCarthy, the Vikings' 2024 first-round pick. McCarthy missed the entirety of his rookie season because of a torn meniscus and was sidelined for seven games last season because of injuries. McCarthy fell to third string this season after the team signed Murray to start and re-signed Wentz as his backup. McCarthy has started only 10 games and has more interceptions (12) than touchdowns (11). But he's well-liked in the Harbaugh family. John Harbaugh's brother, Jim, once lauded McCarthy as the greatest quarterback in Michigan history.
The 10-year veteran has spent more than four seasons with Callahan: three in Cincinnati, when Callahan was the Bengals' coordinator; another in Tennessee, when Callahan was head coach, and this offseason with the Giants. Allen was among the roster cuts late last month.

articles.content_orig:
US Air Force to shut down research centre focusing on Chinese military
The China Aerospace Studies Institute published open-source research on the PLA’s air, space, cyber and missile capabilities
The US Air Force is shutting down a major research centre dedicated to open-source analysis of the Chinese military’s air, space, cyber and missile capabilities.
The China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) said in a statement on Tuesday that Air University, the US Air Force institution under which it operates, had decided to close the institute, with all of its roles becoming unfunded from October 1.
CASI said its employees would continue to work and get paid for now and that it expected to honour its existing commitments “through at least March of 2027”.
The institute will continue publishing articles and reports already in the pipeline and conducting courses on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) that it has already committed to provide to air force units. However, a 10th anniversary event scheduled for February will be cancelled.

articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Hayden Panettiere previously overdosed, secretly entered rehab weeks before death
articles.content_orig:
Hayden Panettiere previously overdosed, secretly entered rehab weeks before death
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Hayden Panettiere allegedly previously overdosed and secretly entered rehab weeks before her drug-related death at an Airbnb in Greenville, South Carolina, on Aug. 16.
On Wednesday, Page Six obtained a more detailed report by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office, which stated that either Brian or Zach Hickerson (the name was redacted) claimed Panettiere had “a long history of drug, alcohol and nitrous oxide abuse” and that he “has had to administer Narcan to the decedent before.”
Narcan is an emergency medication used to reverse opioid overdoses.
The same brother insisted he was “unaware of the decedent using any illegal substances yesterday or today but stated that she was very good at hiding them.”
One of the two Hickersons also said the actress “was in a drug rehab facility in Malibu, California, up until a few weeks ago.”
According to the report, Panettiere’s father, Skip Panettiere, confirmed his daughter “had recently been released [from] rehab” in “Malibu.” He said she spent “two or three weeks” at the treatment facility.
Skip explained Hayden “struggled with addiction since her early 20s and [had] been in multiple rehab facilities since that time.”
He also noted his daughter “suffered from postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter,” Kaya, 11, and said her “addiction issues … escalated since then.”
The grieving dad — who also lost his son, Jansen Panettiere, in February 2023 — made sure to stress that Hayden’s relationship with on-off boyfriend Brian, 37, had been “nothing but troubled.”
According to the report, Skip was adamant about not wanting “any of the decedent’s personal property left with [Brian] or [Zach].” Both Skip and Hayden’s estranged mother, Lesley Vogel, requested her belongings. The exes were notified they had to reach an agreement before the items could be released.
The newly released findings by the coroner’s office, which TMZ was first to report, included previously unknown details about the day the “Heroes” star died at age 36.
“A small clear plastic bag of a white powdery substance in a suitcase belonging to the decendent inside of a gray sunglasses case” was discovered on the scene, as was “a cut straw with residue … inside of a small blue-colored makeup-type bag … inside [a] black bookbag/purse belonging to the decendent.”
Also located inside the apartment was “a medication bottle labeled as Adderall to the decendent on the kitchen table that contained a small clear plastic bag with blue-colored tablets that appeared to possibly be pressed pills and a cut straw.”
Per the report, the pills and straws later tested positive for fentanyl.
Investigators also found “multiple prescription bottles on the kitchen table and a small teal blue-colored lunchbox with glass vials [as well as] prefilled and empty syringes located in the refrigerator.”
The coroner determined Hayden’s death was an “accident” caused by “the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine.”
Naloxone and cotinine were also detected in her system, according to the results of the toxicology.
It was previously know that Brian and Hayden had flown to Greenville from Los Angeles the day before she died. He told responding officers he went to sleep in the bedroom and that Hayden fell asleep in the living room.
According to the new report, Brian said he woke up around 10 or 10:30 a.m. on Sunday and saw the “Nashville” star applying her makeup in the bathroom.
They “ate cereal together” before Brian allegedly “fell back asleep” in the bedroom. He said he woke back up later that afternoon after hearing his brother knock on the front door. The trio had plans to go out to lunch, per the report.
One of the two Hickerson boys (the name was redacted) said he then went to go wake up Hayden, who was “sitting crisscross applesauce, face down and unresponsive on the sofa bed.” She was also “purple in color.”
He stated that “it is not uncommon for the decendent to fall asleep in that position” and claimed he twice administered nasal Narcan “without success.”
The siblings then called 911 and began CPR, which they continued until emergency medical services arrived.
Responding EMS personnel tried for approximately 30 minutes to revive Hayden, but she was not able to regain cardiac activity and was pronounced dead just after 2:30 p.m.
If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s National Helpline at 1-800-662-HELP (4357).

articles.content_orig:
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on August 05, 2026 in New York City.
Michael M. Santiago | Getty Images
U.S. equities fell on Wednesday as Treasury yields marched higher amid concerns among investors that more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve may be coming down the pike.
Declines in utilities, consumer discretionary and communication services stocks led the broader market's fall, with the three sectors shedding more than 1% each.
Equities were weighed down by an increase in Treasury yields, which jumped after the latest purchasing managers' index readings came in hot. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note reached 5.087%, its highest level since July 2007, while the 2-year Treasury note yield hit its highest level since June 2024 at 4.887%.
2-year yield vs. 10-year yield, 1-day
"We have a lot of strength in corporate earnings, but we also have this inflationary pressure, and there's a tug of war there," Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon, said to CNBC, adding that it's "not just oil" that's driving inflation.
"It's broader, and it's particularly in the services sector," he said. "There's no way that the Fed is going to lower rates or pause at this point. Probably we're going to see maybe two, three rate increases."
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday that "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to get inflation under control.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way," he said. "Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded."
Odds that the Fed would hike rates by a quarter percentage point in October stood above 73% following the developments, according to the CME FedWatch tool. That's up from 55.4% a day ago and just 8.8% one month ago.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours during the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York. He described it as a "very good meeting."
Earlier Tuesday in his address to the U.N., Trump said he has a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
In Tuesday's session, the Nasdaq hit a new all-time intraday high and closed at a record, while the Dow finished lower. The S&P 500 was roughly flat, though the index is about 0.8% off from its all-time high.
McDonald's slides to its lowest level since 2022 as growth plan fails to impress
Chris Kempczinski, CEO of McDonald's, speaking with CNBC on Sept. 23rd, 2026.
McDonald's shares fell sharply Wednesday as the company unveiled a new multiyear growth plan alongside a warning from the company that high inflation and flat restaurant traffic are likely to persist.
CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC that the company is "not expecting things to change" as elevated costs and sluggish traffic continue to weigh on the industry.
Investors are not loving it: shares of McDonald's are down more than 5% in midday trading, on pace for their worst day since April 4, 2025 when they fell 5.7% and trading at their lowest levels since October 2022. The move extends a string of weakness: MCD is now on pace for its seventh straight weekly decline, which would mark its longest losing streak since August 2014.
Selig tells CNBC activity on "mentions" contracts are concerning
Michael Selig, President Donald Trump's nominee to serve as Commodity Futures Trading Commission chairman, testifies in a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing on his nomination on Capitol Hill, Nov. 19, 2025.
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that activity on "mentions" contracts are "concerning."
The response comes after the CFTC informed some of its regulated entities on Tuesday that "mentions" contracts, where traders predict what one would say in a speech, televised event or earnings call, are susceptible to manipulation.
"I think a large number of these contracts have issues, and so we're going to take a hard approach in evaluating those," he said.
Selig also told CNBC the federal regulator has a zero tolerance policy on wash trading, after growing concerns that Kalshi has wash trading on its perpetual futures trades. The Wall Street Journal reported the CFTC is looking into the trades.
The chairman also touched on Kalshi's efforts to introduce margin trading to traders. Selig said the CFTC is evaluating the proposal and that it will allow only traders meeting "stringent eligibility criteria" to participate.
10-year Treasury yield scores fresh 19-year high
Treasury yields raced higher on Wednesday as new services and manufacturing sector data increased worry of further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday he expects the central bank will need to raise interest rates further to tame inflation.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way. Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded," he said in remarks for a housing conference in Chicago.
"In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," he added. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that."
Barr labeled last week's quarter percentage point rate hike "important action" for policy that was "out of position" in getting inflation back to the Fed's 2% target.
The remarks came as S&P Global reported that its flash readings on services and manufacturing hit their highest levels since 2021. Price pressures are also surged, posting their highest readings since October 2022.
The three major averages began Wednesday's session in the red.
The S&P 500 lost 0.1% just after the opening bell, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 156 points, or 0.3%.
Worthington Enterprises, KB Home and IonQ among the stocks making moves before the bell
Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket:
Worthington Enterprises – The industrial manufacturing company surged about 16% on an encouraging outlook from leadership. CEO Joseph Hayek said the company is seeing opportunities across its business, "including rapidly growing demand for our engineered [American Society of Mechanical Engineers] tanks used in liquid cooling systems for data centers." First-quarter adjusted earnings and revenue surpassed the Street's estimates, per LSEG.
KB Home – The homebuilder fell more than 1% after projections for fourth-quarter deliveries came in below expectations. Housing gross margins for the current quarter are expected to range between 16% and 16.6%, while analysts polled by LSEG sought 17.2%.
IonQ – The quantum computing stock jumped 12% after IonQ said it tested the industry's first real-time quantum error decoder. The new capability allows for quantum error correction across operations without slowing down execution time, the company said in an announcement.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed mortgages rose to 7.12% from 6.97% for conforming loan balances of 832,750 or less, the MBA said.
Mortgage and refinance applications fell, while the share of applications for adjustable-rate mortgages rose. ARMs can carry a fixed rate for up to 10 years but then adjusts based on where the market is at that time.
— Diana Olick and Michelle Fox
IonQ rallies on major quantum breakthrough
Shares of IonQ popped more than 13% after the company said it successfully tested the first real-time quantum error decoder. This allows for error correction in quantum computers across operations without slowing execution time.

articles.title_orig: Democrats hold midterm lead with independents breaking sharply against Trump
articles.title_zh: Democrats hold midterm lead with independents breaking sharply against Trump
articles.content_orig: By — Matt Loffman Matt Loffman Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-lead-in-new-poll-as-trump-looms-over-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats hold midterm lead with independents breaking sharply against Trump Politics Updated on Sep 23, 2026 9:34 AM EDT — Published on Sep 23, 2026 5:00 AM EDT President Donald Trump's efforts to make the midterm elections a referendum on his presidency appear to be backfiring as Democratic congressional candidates hold a significant lead over Republicans in the latest poll from PBS News, NPR and Marist. More than half of registered voters – 53% – say they would vote for Democratic candidates if the election were today, while 41% prefer Republicans. Independents, who often decide competitive races, favor Democrats by a margin of 25 points. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Driving this sentiment is a president who isn't on the ballot but has asked voters to pretend he is. About 7 in 10 voters acknowledge the president is a factor, one way or another, in their vote for Congress. Just 30% of voters say Trump isn't a factor in their vote. "The Democrats are sitting in a very good place," said Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion. "There's a lot of grumbling in the electorate and a lot of sentiment for changing things around." More than half of registered voters – 53% – say they would vote for Democratic candidates if the election were today, while 41% prefer Republicans. Graphic by Steff Staples/PBS News. Trump bragged of Republicans riding his electoral coattails during his speech to the party's midterm convention in Dallas this month, building his strategy on the premise that voters turn out for him and not for anyone else. His appeal is effective largely among self-identified MAGA supporters; 71% say in this poll that their vote for Congress is mostly a vote for the president. But with absentee and mail voting already underway in a handful of states, the poll suggests Trump's influence may have the opposite effect on other voters. Overall, 45% of registered voters and 54% of independents say their vote will be mostly to express their opposition to Trump. Eight in 10 Democrats are motivated to vote against Trump. Just 24% of voters and 12% of independents say they are voting to show support for the president. "That's devastating," Democratic strategist Joel Payne said. In this political environment, he added, it's expected that political partisans will line up behind their team, but when independents are strongly motivated to vote against one side, "that's significant." The president's own numbers have been frozen for most of the year, with 39% approving of his job performance and 59% disapproving in this latest poll. But that top line understates the asymmetry: More than half of voters – 53% – strongly disapprove of the job he's doing, the highest share recorded by Marist across either of his terms in office, and on par with high voter dissatisfaction with Trump in the aftermath of the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. Congressional Republicans have little room to run from Trump. "It's a nationalized election whether they like it or not," Miringoff said. The president's own numbers have been frozen for most of the year, with 39% approving of his job performance and 59% disapproving in the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll. Graphic by Dan Cooney/PBS News. Thirteen incumbents were defeated in their primaries this year, and dozens of members announced plans to retire or run for another office. Nearly one in five lawmakers who started this Congress will not return for the next one, according to an NPR analysis, driven by record-setting retirements and primary defeats. READ MORE: Rising gas prices frustrate voters. Trump says it's an 'inexpensive price to pay' for the Iran war With gas prices, the war in Iran and other national issues dominating, he said, "it'd be next to impossible" for a congressional candidate to ignore those and focus only on local issues. "It's not believable enough because [Trump's] such a dominant force." "These numbers are concerning to Republicans behind the scenes," Republican strategist Melik Abdul said. Abdul wondered whether the president's luck had run out. "It's almost like he's Icarus," the famous figure from Greek mythology, he said. The question is whether Trump's "gotten a bit too close to the sun this time." Republicans lag in enthusiasm The premise behind Trump's plea to pretend he's on the ballot points to a potential turnout problem among his base. The poll shows few signs that his appeal is closing the enthusiasm gap. Voters overall are highly engaged. Nearly 9 in 10 say they care a great deal or quite a bit about which party controls Congress, and 75% say they're following the midterm elections closely. But the passion tilts toward Democrats. Seventy-six percent of Democrats say they care a great deal who wins Congress, while 67% of Republicans say the same. Additionally, 42% of Democrats are following the election very closely compared to 34% of Republicans. Trump's most loyal supporters match Democrats' fervor. Three-quarters of MAGA supporters care a great deal about the outcome. But the rest of the Republican coalition that Trump is asking to show up is lagging behind. Independents are the least engaged of all, with 30% following the race very closely. Miringoff said that gap is the problem Trump's messaging is trying to solve. "When he's not on the ballot, it doesn't automatically transfer," he said. The calculation Republicans have had to make, he added, is that "the enthusiasm factor for their base is a little soft." History is often unkind to a president in Trump's position File photo: President Donald Trump arrives on stage Sept. 9 at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas. Photo by Evan Vucci/Reuters/File Photo In the last 90 years, the incumbent president's party has lost an average of 27 seats in the House of Representatives and three seats in the Senate in midterm elections, according to a recent UC Santa Barbara analysis. In the 2018 midterm elections during Trump's first term in office, Republicans lost 40 House seats. A Marist poll conducted in September that year found a similar picture of the electorate compared to now. Registered voters preferred Democratic congressional candidates by 12 points, 50% to 38%. That lead narrowed in polling over the following two months, settling at 6 points in the final pre-election survey. Of course, margins seen in September polling are a snapshot of the mood of voters, not a forecast of electoral outcomes. Unprecedented redistricting efforts have also narrowed the field of competitive House races since 2018, blunting the potential size of any wave election. "I don't think 40 seats is remotely in play," Miringoff said. A gain of a dozen House seats would be a good outcome for Democrats, he said. Democrats now lead on issues Republicans used to own Gas prices are shown in Great Neck, New York, on Sept. 17, 2026. Photo by Shannon Stapleton/ Reuters For a party in power, a referendum election would be more survivable if voters still trusted it to handle the toughest issues of governing. They don't, according to this latest poll. Voters say Democrats would do a better job handling the economy, gas prices and foreign policy. On immigration, the Republican edge has evaporated. In what has become an election focused on affordability, 42% of voters say Democrats would do a better job handling the economy while 34% say Republicans. In September 2022, Republicans led on the issue by 15 points, and it was a central issue that propelled Trump back to the White House in 2024. The economic mood beneath the latest
